subtopic: MR. ST. LAURENT-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF MR. LACOMBE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 25

speechtext:
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice): Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege. On Friday last the hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains (Mr. Lacombe) made a speech which was rather difficult to follow. However upon looking at the report I find that at page 4045 of Hansard he is reported to have made this statement:
Je comprends que l'honorable ministre de la Justice, bien qu'il soit un grand avocat, avoeat de la Banque de Montreal, du Pacifique Cana-*djen, de tous les monopoles et de tous les trusts, n'a pas beaucoup d'experience parlementaire.
This is -translated in the annex to Hansard as follows:
I realize that the hon. the Minister of Justice, while he is an outstanding barrister, acting as he does as solicitor for the Bank of Montreal, the Canadian Pacific, and every monopoly and trust, has not much parliamentary experience.
I am not quarrelling with the last part of the hon. -member's statement. To the best [Mr. Maclnnia.l
of my recollection I never, during my thirty-seven years of practice, had the advantage of a single retainer from the Canadian Pacific Railway. I did at times act for the Bank of Montreal, and I did have other clients who were engaged in business affairs of some magnitude, but none of them were -monopolies or trusts. During those years I devoted the whole of my time and attention to the practice of my profession. When I accepted the invitation of the right hon. the Prime Minister to become Minister of Justice I similarly felt that I should give my whole time and attention to the performance of the duties of that office. I severed1 all my connections with each and every one of those who had been my clients theretofore, and I resigned from every board of directors of which I had previously been a member. I have -more than once stated that in public; and I repeat here that the assertion of the hon. -member that I am acting as solicitor for the Bank of Montreal, the Canadian Pacific Railway or any other client, -is absolutely contrary to the facts.
There are other assertions appearing in- the report of the speech of the hon. member which may have to be dealt with, but which might more properly be considered when the horn, member is in his seat.

I had not up to that time observed the remarks to which my colleague referred as well as others and I was not in the house at the time they were made, but I find them in Hansard in the official report of the English translation of speeches delivered in French on the date indicated. The hon. member is not in his seat at the moment, but one statement which he made is so serious that I feel no time should be lost in drawing Your Honour's attention to it and asking that it be dealt with in accordance with the means taken to protect the privileges of this house. The statement to which I refer is as follows:
We have here in the cabinet three new millionaires who have made their money since the war's outbreak. We shall denounce -them at the proper time and place. Fortunes are being built up.
The proper time and place to make a statement of that kind is in this House of Commons with the hon. member simultaneously undertaking to prove the charge, or, if he is unable to do so, to resign his seat in this

speechtext:
I should like to make a statement with regard to the final results of the fourth victory loan campaign.
Total sales of bonds amounted to $1,308,985,500. This represented 2,669,111 subscriptions. These sales were made for payment in cash. The fourth victory loan, like the third victory loan, did not involve the issue of any new bonds against the surrender of maturing securities.
It will be recalled that the total objective for the fourth victory loan was set at $1,100,000,000, and that this objective was split, $500,000,000 for individuals covered by the general canvass and payroll canvass, and $600,000,000 for large investors, mostly business firms and corporations, covered by the special names canvass. Each of these objectives was exceeded.
Combined sales by the general canvass and payroll canvass amounted to $529,641,800, representing 2,661,759 subscriptions. In the special names canvass, 7,352 subscriptions were received for $779,343,700 par value of bonds.
The fourth victory loan was the largest public bond issue in the history of Canada. The outstanding feature of the loan was the tremendous increase in the number and amount of sales to individuals in the general and payroll canvasses.
By way of comparison, I wish to submit the following figures showing the results of each of the four victory loans:

This record of voluntary bond purchases by the public of Canada is tangible and convincing evidence of the united determination of Canadians to win the war-it is a declaration of faith in the future of our country. The impressive record of these loans is also a reflection of the valuable and vital work being done for Canada by the national war finance committee, the organization entrusted by the government with the responsibility of carrying out our wartime public borrowing operations. The tens of thousands of men and women throughout Canada who are associated with this committee may well be proud of their contribution to the steady progress of Canada's wartime savings program.
In the budget speech delivered on March 2, 1943, I referred to the fact that some subscribers to victory loans dispose of their bonds over the period following the termination of the public campaign. I should like to take this opportunity to reiterate the statements I made at that time with regard to this practice.
Victory loan bonds are the property of their individual owners who have the right to sell them at any time they may desire. This right has always existed. No restrictions om the sale of bonds have been considered by the government at any time. When a person buys a victory bond, that person is making it possible for Canada to get the men and materials needed for war use, and, in addition, is helping
Fourth Victory Loan

to fight the home-front battle against inflation. When people sell their bonds, they are withdrawing this help. I recognize the fact that emergency needs for cash are perfectly legitimate reasons for selling bonds or presenting war savings certificates for redemption provided the person has no other form of savings which can be used, or provided the person cannot obtain a temporary loan, to be repaid out of future income, to meet the immediate need for cash. But sales of bonds to get dollars to buy things that are not essential are not justifiable. Unless it is absolutely necessary to sell victory bonds, it is every person's patriotic duty, and in his own best interests, to hold on to his bonds for the duration of the war at least. Buying bonds is important; holding on to them is equally important.
On February 9, 1943, I tabled a statistical compilation showing a classification of the sources of subscriptions, at time of issue, to the first, second and third victory loans. For the information of the house, I am tabling a statement in similar form showing the estimated derivation of subscriptions, at time of issue, to the fourth victory loan, together with comparable figures for the three previous victory loans.
All figures in regard to the fourth victory loan are subject to final verification on the receipt of reports of actual deliveries by banks, trust and loan companies. The figures which I have used and which appear in the statement I have tabled reflect the final reports received in Ottawa from the field organization of the national war finance committee.

The class designated individuals includes two sub-divisions, described as "special names" and "all others". These data have been compiled by the national war finance committee from information obtained at the time of public offering of the loans, and from other sources. 1.	What are the names of the members of the national film board?
2.	What is the organizational set-up of the board; how many are employed, and in what position?
3.	How many films have been released to, (a) motion picture theatres; (b) for other use?

5.	What remuneration has been received from motion picture theatres for use of films up to May 31, 1943?
6.	What was the total cost of the national film board, and its work for each year of its operation?
Mr. LaFLECHE: Mr. Speaker, in asking that this question be made an order for a return, there is a reservation in regard to part 5 of the question, which has been explained to the hon. member for Macleod.

An explanation may have been given to the hon. member for Macleod, but this is a question in which the whole house is interested. I would ask the minister to indicate the special reasons for the reservation.
Mr. LaFLECHE: The point is that the national film board advise me that it would not be in the public interest to give figures of rentals received from motion picture 	.1
theatres for the use of the board's films, because, they say, it would be of assistance to the board's competitors.

I protest and raise an objection. I am going to ask the minister to remove his reservation with respect to part 5 of the question, because it asks for information which the house is entitled to have. Certainly "in the public interest" is being stretched to cover matters which this house should not allow.
Mr. LaFLECHE: The remarks made by the leader of the opposition raise an interesting point. This is not the first time that this has been done since I have been in the house-The point is that the national film board is in some respects in competition with commercial companies; it is in the national interest that they have full right to make as good a bargain as they can, and they should not be put in a disadvantageous position by reason of information being made public. -I shall be glad to give the hon. member privately the reasons for the reservation, as I have done to the hon. member for Macleod. It is the position taken by the national firm board that makes necessary the reservation. I think it is the traditional position taken by them.

That explanation is not good enough. This is a government board. These figures refer to national revenue and' national expenditure; surely we are not going to vacate our position in matters of that kind. Who set up the national film board to say what is and what is not in the public interest? Parliament should decide that.

As this question stands in my name and I happen to be in my seat, perhaps I may have a word. One of the officials approached me with respect to part 5 of the question and explained what the minister has already explained to the house. I can see that the point is not one of public expenditure but rather the question whether the amounts received by the film board) from motion picture companies, as a result of its films being shown, should be made public. I readily understood that perhaps it might not be in the public interest to reveal these figures to the board's competitors who are in the motion picture business. Having been advised that I would receive the information for my personal use, I assumed the same thing would apply to every member, so that the information would not necessarily become public property. Under these conditions I agreed that there should be a reservation with respect to part 5 of the question.

Questions

I am going to ask the h'on. member and the minister to allow this question to stand. I think there should be opportunity for consideration of the matter. The minister is going entirely too far when he suggests that the national film board shall determine for the House of Commons and the Canadian people what information it is in the public interest to produce. Largely upon that principle I am going to ask the minister to allow the question to stand, so that further consideration can be given to it. I am sure the Prime Minister will agree that we must not lightly create any precedent on a principle of this kind).

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:

He did not take the responsibility of saying whether the board was right or wrong. I think my hon. friend the leader of the opposition is quite right in raising the point he does and in asking that the question should stand; later the minister might answer it on his own responsibility.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext: The house resumed from Friday, June 25, consideration in committee of a resolution to grant to his majesty certain sums of money for the carrying out of measures consequent upon the existence of a state of war-Mr. Tlsley-Mr. Donnelly in the chair.
Vocational training of discharged members of Canada's armed forces, $525,000.

I was not here during the latter part of the session on Friday evening. Am I to understand that the general discussion on this resolution, so far as it lelates to the Department of Labour, has been completed?
Yes.
And therefore it would not be in order to discuss a particular item until it is called?
That is right. '
Then I will sit down.

Before this item carries, the question of vocational training of discharged members of Canada's armed forces requires something more than simply the passing of an item. It has to do with a subject in which there is more than usual interest throughout the dominion, and one which forms a vital part of the whole rehabilitation programme and the plan for settling and rehabilitating out men when the war is over.

The vocational training of discharged members of Canada's armed forces, and the plans which have been made in connection therewith, may I think properly form the subject of some consideration by this committee at this time, because on many occasions complaints have been made by the public with regard to the manner in which men who have been discharged from the armed forces are being treated in Canada. I realize that perhaps in many instances these reports are without foundation, but it is most important that the government should see to it that, of all classes of our people to whom attention is paid at this time, consideration is given to discharged members of the armed forces, because of the fact that they constitute the major section of the population and, further, because of the sacrifices they are prepared to make on behalf of the country. I should like the minister to indicate to the committee what the plans are with respect to this vocational training. If the minister will give me his attention'-
I am giving it. Don't worry.

I would ask the minister to give the committee the benefit of his information with regard to the number of discharged soldiers who have either begun or have been offered or have completed training under this particular item. What plans are contemplated for the future? Will the minister also give some information as to the type of vocational training which the government has in mind for men who have been discharged from the armed forces?

As my hon. friend is probably aware, the Labour department merely takes care of training through the instrumentality of the training section of the department. Up to date 1.200 returned men have been trained or are being trained. The course of training is similar to that undertaken- under the general training scheme. There is a choice on the part of the -men for the kind of training they wish to undertake, and I need hardly tell my hon. friend that it is simply a matter of training them and putting them to work, because there is n,o dearth of employment, as there was following the last war, after training is completed. The real problem will come when the war is over, but plans are laid under the act passed last year to set in motion policies that will have for their purpose the training of men discharged from the armed forces at the conclusion of the war.

War Appropriation-Labour

I am sorry the Minister of Mines an.d Resources is not in his place, because I had a communication this morning from a returned veteran in British Columbia who applied in November last for an allotment under the land settlement scheme. He has never heard a word about it since. Is that the kind of attention the Department of Labour will give returned veterans?
If any member of this house has knowledge of delay in connection with the training of any veteran who has returned from this war, I shall be glad to hear about it.

I have made an inquiry of the department in regard to a mam who desired to go on, the land, and I have been informed that the department is being organized by provinces and that all the provinces are not yet organized, so that men who are applying from some provinces may not yet have received word.
What are you-an apologist for the department?
The member for \rork-Sunbury has told of his experience with the department, and I have just as much right to tell of my experience.

On a question of privilege, I did not refer to my own experience but to the experience of a veteran. I have taken the matter up in a courteous way with the associate director and I have no doubt I shall get a satisfactory explanation.

May I continue to tell of my experience with the department? I have inquired with reference to men who are now serving in the imperial army. In fact, some of them have been taken prisoner, and it is my information from officials of the department that they will evolve a plan under which men who are now serving in the imperial forces and also in the Canadian forces will be given an opportunity when they return to go on the land. In all my dealings with the department I have had nothing but prompt replies.
I have had one or two inquiries with regard to this-

On a point of order, I
have nothing whatever to do with, the farm settlement scheme, and there is nothing in these estimates of mine dealing with it. I
suggest that if members have questions with reference to that scheme, they wait until the Minister of Mines and Resources is here.

What I have to say does
not happen to refer to farming. It is another matter. These men who have returned are anxious to know how to proceed in order to take advantage of this opportunity, and I think a great deal of publicity should be given to the regulations. I was going to ask the minister what publicity they are being given, and what percentage of the men already discharged have made application for training. I believe a very small percentage of those who would like to take advantage of it have made application.

I meant to point out in replying to the leader of the opposition that the returned men in question are referred to us by the Department of Pensions and National Health. If my memory serves me correctly, about 93,000 men have been discharged from the armed forces, and as I indicated a moment ago, 1,200 are receiving training under the auspices of the Department of Labour. In view of the comparative ease with which a job can be obtained at the present time it appears to us that most of the men who have been discharged from the armed forces do not bother much about training, because they can get a job without it. I suppose it is the natural thing to do.
Are the men given any choice? Is it not up to the department to see that they have the opportunity to take advantage of this training?

I understand, then, that
in the mines and resources estimates there will be an item similar to this; or will they work on part of this vote?

What I meant was
that I have no jurisdiction over the soldier settlement plan.

No portion of this money
is used for that plan?
No, none at all.

The minister has mentioned a fact that is well known to all of us-that most of these discharged men are able to find work. But suppose a man does not wish to stay at that work for the rest of his life; suppose he wants to get training for some other type of
War Appropriation-Labour

work. Can he get any assistance as long as he is employed? I have received complaints to the effect that if a discharged soldier is working he is not eligible for assistance. For example, could he get help to enable him to go to night school, or to take a correspondence course, or to get training in some other way for an occupation different from that in which he happens to be engaged at the present time?

Of course there are what are called vocational advisers attached to the major offices under the unemployment insurance commission, and when a returned man' wants training, his case is investigated by one of these vocational guidance officers. I do not know why he would be refused that assistance, because we are only too anxious to get people to train.
If a discharged man has a job and is working, can he get help in order to train for some other job?
Yes, he could attend evening classes; there is no objection to that.
Is the minister sure that man would get financial help in order to attend classes in the evening, for example?

Of course my hon. friend understands that it would have to be an approved course. If the man took these evening classes in his spare time, as many civilians do, I should not think he would expect to get paid twice.
But will the department pay for his tuition at that evening class?
Absolutely.
And will the department pay for a correspondence course?
It has to be an approved course. At the moment I could not go as far as to include a correspondence course.
Where are these training classes held?
At vocational and technical schools all over the country.
I do not suppose agriculture is included in these trades and occupations?
As yet we have not established any classes in agriculture for returned soldiers.

Reference was made a few 'moments ago to the Veterans' Land Act. I understood from what took place in the committee that certain training would be given

to soldiers when they came home if they wanted to go on the land. Would that be included under this item?
While at the moment we are not following the suggestion of my hon. friend, I am sure if there should be a need for classes of the kind mentioned we would be prepared to develop them.
Is any of this money to be used to enable university students whose courses have been interrupted by the war to go on with their training?
That comes under the next item.
I thought the next item was for assistance to the universities in meeting extra costs in accelerating courses.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: And in providing loans to certain students.
That covers the sort of thing I have in mind, then?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Yes.

Personally I am not quite satisfied with the explanation given by the minister in regard to the vocational training provided for men discharged1 from the army. I believe the machinery provided for that purpose is anything but satisfactory. There is a great deal of delay, and' many factors militate against the man who returns from the armed forces. As I understand the machinery now provided, it is strictly of an emergency nature; the training given to-day is for the purpose of fitting a man to go immediately into industry. In other words a man is given a short course which will enable him to take his place in war industry. I do not visualize that as a satisfactory vocational training programme for the future, though it may be all right now, to meet a temporary need. The machinery provided to enable the man to get in touch with a vocational training officer is also unsatisfactory. Let me take my own province as an example. There is one welfare officer for the whole province, who sits in with the unemployment insurance officers in Halifax. It is necessary to get through to him in order to make application to take advantage of the regulations as they now exist, and many of the boys coming out of the service have no knowledge of this officer. Men who have been out of the army for three or four months have written me to find out how to go about getting this training, and there is a great deal of delay in getting in touch with this one welfare

War Appropriation-Labour
officer. Most of the men coming out of the army are forced to take whatever employment is offered, in order to live.
If a discharged soldier desires to take advantage of these arrangements for vocational training, he is informed that he must present himself at a certain centre. This may mean that he will have to go three, four or five hundred miles from where his family lives. During the time he is taking that course he receives $14.40 a week if he is a married man. That is not sufficient to pay his board while taking the course and at the same time maintain his family in another part of the country. This situation is peculiar to Nova Scotia. I do not know what the arrangement is in the other provinces, but many more men would take advantage of vocational training if some provision were made for subsistence allowances while they were taking their courses. Many men who have been discharged from the army are in industry only temporarily, and later on the job of reestablishment will have to be done all over again.
I have a suggestion to offer to the minister which may be worthy of consideration. To-day, particularly in central Canada, there are some plants which are going out of war production; I would direct attention particularly to Research Enterprises Limited in Toronto, a technical plant which has been making certain instruments. Parts of these plants are going out of production. Employees are being taken' completely out of them and placed in other essential lines. These plants are equipped1 to do certain jobs. They could easily be converted back into training machinery so that the plant might be utilized following the war. People could be trained to do a job which would be of permanent benefit to them.
I suggest the minister will have to give consideration to the matter of remuneration, especially if he expects returned soldiers to take vocational training. Provision will have to be made for the families of these men while they are living away from home. In Nova Scotia they are trained in New Glasgow, or in New Brunswick in Moncton, and they have to travel four or five hundred miles from their homes, maintaining themselves and their families at the same time. It is all right in an emergency to have men enter a war industry, but a permanent arrangement must be made for the time after the war.

Of course, as I said before, the Department of Pensions and National Health merely turn the returned soldiers over to us for training. No doubt the minister of that department will take note of the hon. member's observations. With respect to
using the buildings now used by Research Enterprises Limited, may I point out that at this very moment conversations are going on between officials of my department and those of the Department of Munitions and Supply with that end in view.
Mr. MoCANN: Where discharged members of the Canadian armed forces take advantage of facilities offered by vocational and technical schools which are maintained by the various municipalities, does the assistance go to the individual or to the institution? If it goes to the individual, on what ground; and what are his prospective expenses in connection with it? I ask these questions in view of the fact that these institutions are maintained by local communities.

The payments go to the individual. We pay any additional cost in the community. For instance, a municipality may give us a school. In some instances we share the costs, and in others we pay all the costs. We may pay the salaries of extra teachers.

What is the position of a man who gets his discharge now and takes a job in a war industry which, after he has worked there a year or year and a half, closes down? Will he then be able to get vocational training for another job?

We have not yet been faced with that situation, but the hon. member may rest assured that at least while I am minister we shall try to do the sensible thing.
Mr. MacNIC'OL: I should like to ask one or two questions with respect to vocational training. I refer to the returned men who are sent to factories or schools for such training. For instance, does anyone from the minister's department with authority to inspect make any follow-up to ascertain how these people are taught?
We have regional directors in each province. They in turn have inspectors who look over the work that is being done.

I am particularly concerned with the large increase in accidents in factories, particularly in Ontario. I refer to that province, because it is a report from Ontario which I hold in my hand. Are the men who have been called to these factories receiving adequate protection? If they are not used to working in plants they are much more likely to have accidents than if they had been trained in industrial .plants. The statements with respect to accidents are alarming. For instance, the Toronto Evening
War Appropriation-Labour

Telegram of June 25, 1943, contains a report in which figures issued by the Industrial Accident Prevention Association are given. The report shows that there has been an increase in accidents to the extent of five per cent, and that the number of accidents in May reached the alarming figure of 10,320, of which 26 were fatalities. Then, $937,649 was paid out by the workmen's compensation board in May of this year. These are figures for the province of Ontario alone, I believe, and they are very bad indeed. If they apply in equal proportion throughout Canada the total would be a matter of serious concern.
It must be remembered that many of the young men who went overseas and were there for two or three years had not done a day's work in industry before their enlistment, because many of them had not had employment during the depression period. What training are those men to be given? Unless they are taught how to prevent the loss of fingers, or to avoid being struck on the head or having a foot smashed, they may be the victims of accidents. If precautions are not taken, many Canadians will be handicapped, not only by injuries sustained in the war, but by those sustained subsequently as the result of industrial accidents.
The workmen's compensation board will not carry them on indefinitely. If the department has established means of training these inexperienced men in factories, it should see to it that they are protected against themselves. I have had a long experience in industry, and I have learned that accidents take place very easily. I know that various governments have inspectors who endeavour to surround machinery and other industrial hazards with every possible protection. Perhaps the time has arrived when the federal department of labour should step in and see to it that men sent to factories for training purposes are safeguarded against accidents.

I too have noticed the increase in the number of industrial accidents. I suppose that is the natural result of the tremendous expansion in industry. Many are entering industry for the first time. As to these trainees of ours, so far as I know we have not had a serious accident in the last year. My hon. friend is aware of course that workmen's compensation is under provincial jurisdiction, and operates in all the provinces. In most of the provinces, if not indeed all of them, there are accident prevention associations, or organizations of a similar type, financed by industry on an assessment basis. We have indicated to the provincial workmen's compensation boards this alarming increase in the number of accidents. fMr. MacNicol.]
Your department has, do you say?

Yes, our department has. But I think the hon. member will agree with me that the matter of factory supervision and legislation pertaining thereto comes within the four corners of property and civil rights, and that it is far better to use the instrument already built up than to have the federal Department of Labour enter the field of its own accord. In Ontario they have a most efficient accident prevention association. Naturally the worker is conscious of any loss of earning power, and that possible loss is an incentive to him to take some interest in accident prevention. The employer is interested, too, because his assessment with respect to workmen's compensation goes up and down according to the accident rate.
Under our training plan, in some centres we conduct classes in first aid. I believe that is at least a contribution, possiblj' not to the actual prevention of accidents, but to the lessening of the results of accidents. We know that sometimes workmen do not take that degree of care in respect to the possibility of minor accidents that they should. A workman may cut his finger and let it go without the necessary attention, and this may result in something serious, such as blood poisoning. For a great many years I took a keen interest in workmen's compensation in Ontario, and I have served on many committees set up by the labour movement which waited upon the Ontario government to ask for amendments to the workmen's compensation act of that province. While I have not the figures before me, I think it can be said that within the period of a generation there has been almost a transformation in the approach to the prevention of industrial accidents and disease. There has-been a tremendous improvement over what existed twenty-five years ago. While I regret along with my hon. friend the increase which has taken place, I think it is one of those things that you cannot control, especially when you consider the tremendous expansion in industry which has taken place and the fact that so many people have entered industry for the first time.
How long does a man have to be in the service before he is eligible for this grant?
If he has an honourable discharge I think he could get it at any time.
Is there any stated time?

Not to my knowledge.

War Appropriation-Labour
If he is in only one day, he would get it?

As I pointed out, these men are sent to me by the Department of Pensions and National Health. If a man had never been in the army or the navy or the air force we should be glad to train him for industry.

I have had a little trouble in getting a case settled with the Department of Pensions and National Health. The particulars of this case have a direct bearing upon the item before the committee. The Department of Pensions and National Health refused to make a rehabilitation grant to this man because he had not been in the service the required six months, and the whole case turned upon whether his length of service would date from the day he was sworn in or from the day he was first on full pay in the service. This point should be definitely settled, because I have no doubt the minister will have to deal with similar cases. I should like to read a paragraph from a memorandum of the Department of Pensions and National Health under date of June 24, 1943, with reference to this man. It reads:
This man, after less than six months actual active service, was discharged from the forces whilst in Deer Lodge hospital, Winnipeg, on February 17, 1942, following treatment for rheumatic fever. As he had less than 183 days active service, he is not eligible for the rehabilitation grant of thirty days' pay.
The Minister of National Defence for Air stated definitely in the house that the man was actually in the service from the day he was sworn in, but when this case comes up before the Department of Pensions and National Health the question arises whether his service would date from the day he was attested or from the day he began to draw full pay in the service. This point is not clear from what has been said by the Minister of National Defence for Air and the Minister of Pensions and National Health.

I thought I made it clear that the handling of men after they are discharged is not a function of the Department of Labour, that it comes under the jurisdiction of the Department of Pensions and National Health. If my hon. friend will give me the correspondence I shall be glad to get in touch with that department and try to get an answer for him.
Is it not the minister's department that makes these grants?

The Department of
Pensions and National Health send the men to us and we train them.
The minister would have to refer back to the Department of Pensions and National Health to find out whether a man was eligible?
We do not come into the picture until it is decided that a man is to be trained.
I suppose this question would properly come up under Department of Pensions and National Health?
That is right.

That is
where we are having the difficulty.

I am not clear, and there are many discharged men who are not clear as to the procedure which should be followed in order for a discharged man to be considered eligible for this training. First, will the minister tell the committee what the procedure is? Second, will the minister make clear the nature of the assistance which is being given to these returned men? That should be done for the benefit of the men themselves. Third, how many men are now receiving vocational training, and where are they receiving it? I realize that there may be considerable difficulty at the present time when a few men are being trained here and a few more in another part of the country, but I should like to know just what classes are being' set up and where this training is available. Next, what is the nature of the vocational training classes that are available for returned men? Next, have the government given any consideration to studying the future industrial needs of the country? Our technical schools spend a lot of money on training pupils for jobs which do not exist when the training is completed, for vocations which have become more or less obsolete. Considering the technological changes that are occurring I assume the government are making sure that they know what the needs of industry will be when this training is completed.

First, my hon. friend
asked how a returned soldier should go about getting this training. He would get in touch with the rehabilitation officer in his locality. In the larger centres this man is to be found in the unemployment insurance offices. Next, my hon. friend asked what allowances are being given. They vary from $7 to $18 a week according to the circumstances. He

War Appropriation-Labour

asked how many are being trained. At present there are twelve hundred. He asked where they are being trained and what training they are receiving. I have not that information in front of me, but I shall endeavour to get it before these estimates have been completed. Next, he asked if these people are being trained so that they will fit into the post-war picture. That is a pretty hard question to answer.
What steps is the government taking to ascertain what will be the means?

My hon. friend will appreciate that it is the function of the James committee to advise the government in that direction. Then there is the Macintosh committee and a committee of this house on rehabilitation and ipost-war problems. It is a difficult question to answer. A mam may learn a trade to-day,, and with a shift in styles or in the wants of the (people, that trade may be obliterated almost overnight. It is difficult to indicate the industrial structure of the post-war period. A committee of the House of Commons is at this very moment giving study to the question my hon. friend raises.

How is information given to the discharged soldier, a man out in a small village, for instance, as to the officer to whom he should apply, the location of his office, and so forth, if the soldier wants to take vocational training?

He is told that upon discharge. I do not think the average soldier passes much up. That was my experience in the last war, and I think the hon. member for Cape Breton South will agree with me. We had a pretty good idea of what we were entitled to and where we were going.
Mr. GILL.IS: That has been the theory, but the fact is that the soldiers are not getting the information.

This is a very important subject, and there is a suggestion I should like to make to the minister and to the committee in connection with vocational training. When hostilities end, under the present plans of the united nations there will be occupation of friendly countries now overrun by the axis, as well as the occupation of enemy countries. I am going to make a plea for a system of vocational training to meet the needs of the period immediately after the war and until the signing of the peace treaty. I think I ought to get considerable support for the suggestion from the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Labour, 
who has given many years to the study of international affairs and who is the distinguished vice-president for Canada of the Institute of Foreign Affairs.
During the past several months in the United States, as in Great Britain, consideration is being given to the post-war period when there will be occupancy of various countries from the cessation of hostilities to the signing of the peace treaty. The experience after the last war in the matter of occupation of countries was not everything it should have been. Only recently I was reading an article on this subject which quoted Colonel Hunt, who was the United States officer in charge of the occupation of Germany in 1919 and 1920. He states in,, "American Military Government of Occupied Germany, 1918-20":
All of the energy of the American army had been centered1 on an early decision in the field, and there had been no opportunity to study the civil problems involved in an occupation of German territory. The American army therefore began its duties in occupied territory with only the scantiest information both of the particular situation confronting it and even of a broader nature, such as would permit it to intelligently frame an organization commensurate with its wride governmental powers. From the beginning there was a crying need for personnel trained in civil administration and possessing knowledge of the German nation.
The United States has already seen the necessity of doing something in. this regard and has started schools for the training of civilian administrators and other officers who will be in charge of civil affairs in the occupied territories.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: My hon. friend is referring to the school in Virginia, for instance?

Yes, that is one.
Two types of government will be set up, one a military government and the other a civil government. The United States in consultation with the other united nations has practically concluded that as soon as possible after occupancy takes place of an area in friendly countries now occupied by the axis, the military government should give way to a civil government, and that there should be placed in charge of those areas men from the various united nations who have been trained in civil administration. A number of articles have been written on the subject.
When occupation takes place a wide range of social and rehabilitation activities will be required. Civilian administrators will be needed who have training and experience in such matters as public health and housing, and a knowledge of the territory occupied. Furthermore, under the present scheme, educational institutions will be set up in the

War Appropriation-Labour
occupied areas and a system of re-education will be set up in Germany and the other axis nations in order to indicate to these people the falsity of the teachings they have followed during the last thirty or forty years. The united nations will show them through education that men in all the countries of the earth can live in amity one with another. The falsity of the doctrine of blood and iron and aggression which has resulted in two wars in our lifetime will be terminated by such a system of education. But to that end trained men will be necessary. As the minister's parliamentary assistant mentioned a little while ago, schools have been opened in Virginia, and in other states of the United States schools are to be established to train men for this work. They will have to be carefully trained and will require a comprehensive course of study. These men will be selected according to their ability, their character, and their maturity and powers of leadership.
Some time ago Mr. Sumner Welles in the United States said that for a period of some years after hostilities ceased - possibly five years-there would be no peace treaty signed until a settlement had been arrived at and peaceful relations restored among the nations of the world. I make this suggestion to the minister, who I know will do everything he can to train our men for a vocation when they retu-n from overseas, to give them an opportunity to take their place in the post-war world, when it may be anticipated that some of the economic difficulties that arose after the last war will again rear their heads in our midst and employment for our service men will again be a problem to be solved. We do not want to have men returning after this war to conditions such as those to which the last generation returned. Now is the time to set'up in Canada a school of civil administration complementary to the school which is operating in the United States. It would mean that several thousand service men-I would say, at the beginning, five or six thousand of them- would receive training in civil administration. They will have served their country in time of war, and possibly many of them will be prevented by war disabilities from doing physical wrork. By setting up a school of this kind Canada will be enabled to take her place in the sphere of international affairs and exercise her influence in a larger way than she did before the war. The first proceeding will be the setting up of a training school; then, later, will come the training of these men, which will assure them of employment for several years after the close of hostilities, and
will supply them with training which will stand them in exceptionally good stead when they return to civilian life.
I realize that what I suggest is an innovation, but since the outbreak of this war there have been many breaks with tradition. After the last war it would not have occurred to anyone to establish schools of this kind. The United States is finding that the system is working out, and a skeleton organization should be set up in Canada at once. The necessary personnel for training is available. We have in the armed forces men who are informed on public health, social service, eduestion and the like: suitable educational staffs exist in the army. I feel that if this suggestion were implemented, many thousands of our men who might otherwise be debarred from post-war employment because of disabilities will be assured of occupation for several years in work which will be necessary for the preservation of the peace of the world. Canada must take a larger (place than ever before in international affairs after the war, and the adoption of this plan will train men to take their part in the new world.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) has referred to a matter which the department from one point of view has seriously been considering. The question of training men of the armed services and others at the end of the war or during the wTar to take assignments in what we hope will be the occupied areas of Europe and Asia is not entirely, in fact it is only very remotely, a matter in which this department from an initial point of view can be said to be interested. In this country the question of training men and women for service in Europe and Asia at the end of the war is itself dependent upon policy of a higher order. In the first instance there will be the question of the proportion of appointments as between the various members of the victorious powers. There will be the question of the wisdom of having, let us say, Canadians or Englishmen or Americans serving in an administrative capacity in some of the European states and one will have to consider the psychological factor in relation to that sort of thing. However, as the hon. member has mentioned, in the United States considerable attention is being paid to this subject. There are schools in Virginia, at the university of Michigan at Ann Arbor, at Portland, Oregon, and in Washington. These at the moment are largely under the department of war or such military departments as have to do with the conduct of the war. The course of training presupposes qualifications which are
72537-259^
War Appropriation-Labour

not those of the average person, and it is doubtful, in view of the training which most members of the armed forces now have, whether any considerable number could take advantage of the course.
However, the hon. member has, I think, done a great service in bringing the matter to public attention, I believe for the first time in this country. A committee of the Department of Labour is considering these matters; and, to the extent that this may be regarded in any sense as a problem of the department-and primarily it cannot be said to be such-the hon. member can be assured, knowing the interest of the minister and myself in these matters, that it will be given not only the best possible consideration, but the closest attention.

I want to refer back to the discussion which was pursued a few minutes ago about the allowance provided for men who are discharged and are taking training while they are away from home. I notice that order in council P.C. 2/3241, passed on April 20, provides, in the first paragraph of section 11, as follows:
The minister may pay to a person pursuing a course under the provisions of paragraph (6) hereof and who is (1) a married person or (2) a person in respect of whom an additional allowance for dependents is being paid under this order, a living allowance of five dollars per week for any week whilst he is necessarily living away from his usual place of residence in pursuing such course and is thereby, in the opinion of the minister, obliged to incur extra living expenses.
It does seem to me that these government regulations, whether relating to this or any other type of allowance, are never framed with a view of giving the men every possible advantage. Perhaps the minister's department is not to blame. The treasury department sit above or behind them and they whittle away, whittle away, until the rules have been written up with such meticulous care that not one penny more is given than will provide anything beyond bare necessities. I fail to see how $5 a week is adequate for a man living away from home. Let me ask the minister two questions. First, does he think that $5 a week is really sufficient for a man living away from home?
Some get $25 a day.

Yes, but they are not discharged veterans. I do not know whether any of these men are taking training in Ottawa. I do not think that Ottawa is any different from any other city when it comes to housing congestion and the cost of living.
{Mr Martin.]
That being so, can the minister tell us where we can get board and room in Ottawa for $5 a week? If he can, that information will be very useful even to members of parliament, who have no exemptions for expenses, and I am quite certain it will be very useful to civil servants who get just enough salary to get by on, provided they can obtain room and board at the cheapest possible place. Will the minister answer those two questions?

In the first place I have no jurisdiction over allowances to soldiers; it does not come under my department. All that my department does is to train people. That question would come under the estimates of the department of pensions.
I do not blame the minister for evading that question.

That is getting to be the regular answer now, and it does seem to me that the coordination of the various departments is such that when you ask one minister a question he can easily say that it comes under another minister, and when you ask that other minister the same question he says that it comes under the items dealt with by another department. It is a case of playing tag with the various ministers and passing the buck. Perhaps the question does not come under this department, but does the minister think that $5 a week is a sufficient allowance? Perhaps he does not, but has he brought influence to bear upon his colleague the minister of pensions to have a little more given to these men?-who, remember, enlisted in the army. They volunteered to sacrifice everything and are now discharged, some of them perhaps because of ill health. Not being in receipt of pension, thgse brave lads are asked to take some course of training, and we think we are doing wonders for them w-hen we give them $5 a week to live on.
Ask the humanitarians.

A few moments ago we were discussing the question whether discharged men could take correspondence courses. It so happens that this morning I had a file sent to me from Vancouver. I did not have it in my hands at the time of the discussion, but I have it now. This man had served three and a half years in Canada, eventually becoming company quartermaster sergeant. On his discharge, category E, he obtained a position with the dominion civil service as a grade 4 clerk in the Dominion of Canada assay office in Vancouver, but it was pointed out to him at the time that the job was only a temporary one because

War Appropriation-Labour
the man who held it had enlisted for work which would not result in his becoming a casualty; in other words he would come back upon the conclusion of the war; so that my informant has known all the time that he had only a temporary job. That being the fact, he applied to the veterans' welfare officer for assistance in taking a correspondence course in the International Accountants Society Incorporated. His plan was eventually to write an examination which would give him a degree from the Canadian General Accountants association. The cost of the course was $140.25. He was advised by the welfare officer to write to Lieutenant-Colonel F. T. Fairey, a provincial government employee in Victoria, but also regional director of the war emergency training programme. I have here a letter from Colonel Fairey in reply, one paragraph of which reads:
I must say, however, that under the present regulations I have no authority to pay fees for correspondence courses of any kind, either as an official of the provincial government or as regional director of the war emergency training programme. If, as you know, you were taking vocational training under post-discharge order P.C. 7633, I then would be responsible for the cost of your training during the time you were drawing subsistence allowances, but no provision is made for the type of instruction you suggest.
In other words, the man would have to be out of work and be a charge on the government for subsistence allowance before anything could be done for him. Only by being out of work could he get assistance in taking that course. That is directly opposite to what the minister told the committee when the subject was discussed a few minutes ago. It is true that this letter is dated March 17, and perhaps there has been another order in council since that time. However, this discharged veteran again saw the veterans' welfare officer and wrote to what is known as the district rehabilitation board in Vancouver. I have here a letter from them dated May 6 of this year, from which I quote the following:
The local rehabilitation board has considered your request for a correspondence course in accountancy under order in council P.C. 7633. However, the writer regrets to inform you that the board does not consider it advisable to make a grant for this purpose owing to the fact that you have had considerable experience, that you are now employed in a relatively good position and that this course is not therefore necessary for your rehabilitation.
This letter shows that, regardless of what the Department of Labour here may think, this rehabilitation board in Vancouver is not in favour of granting assistance for courses of this type, and I suggest that the last-mentioned ground is a most unreasonable one, namely, that it is not ncessary for this man's rehabilitation.
Here is a man in a temporary job-and there must be thousands of others in the same position, for example men who work in war industries but are obviously there only temporarily. Perhaps they would like to have some training that would fit them for permanent work, but the point of view of this board is that help cannot be given in a case of this kind. I would ask the minister not only to assure the committee that this rehabilitation board is wrong and that correspondence courses can be given, but to go further and indicate that decision to the various boards across Canada. When men receive treatment of this kind, in most cases they are knocked out; they are through; they do not keep coming back, because they believe it is hopeless and that they cannot get help; they are-dissatisfied and it makes for discontent throughout the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Can the hon. member give me the details privately ?

Yes. I will give the minister the file. This is a matter that should be made absolutely clear. A discharged veteran, in order to get help, should not necessarily be out of work but should be able to get help so that he may become permanently established.

I am sorry if I misinformed my hon. friend; I did not intend to. The labour department has not yet established the principle of paying for correspondence courses with private organizations im connection with the training programme. I want to make that clear. I am not trying to* evade the issue, as has been suggested, bufc this matter does not come under the jurisdiction of my department. It comes under the minister of pensions. My department has to do with training for trades and callings, more than the sort of thing mentioned by my hon. friend.
Suppose a man is working in the day time on a war job and wants to take training in some trade in the evenings. Can he get that or can he not?
Of course we have part time evening courses, which are free, but there is no allowance paid in connection with those. Men and women work during the day and. go to those classes in the evening.
They are employed during the day.
Yes.
Then the department will pay for their tuition in the evening?

Oh, absolutely.
War Appropriation-Labour
There is no doubt about that?
No doubt at all.

There is another
point regarding discharged members of the armed forces. I do not see anything here which would enable a soldier to continue his education which was interrupted because of the war.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: If I may interrupt the hon. gentleman, education comes under my department entirely and can be thoroughly discussed either on the war appropriation or the departmental estimates. I can assure my hon. friend that most comprehensive arrangements have been made both for ordinary education and for post-graduate courses for soldiers when they are discharged. I do not want to hold up the estimates of my colleague at the moment; later I shall be very glad to give my hon. friend all information on that point.
I just wanted to ask whether education came under the Department of Labour or the Department of Pensions and National Health.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Although the actual work of vocational training is being carried out at the present time under the Department of Labour there is in addition a most comprehensive programme of vocational training being arranged in my department. A director of vocational training has been appointed, and I shall be glad to explain fully to my hon. friend what is being done in regard to both vocational training and education under my department.
Then the next item does not cover the sort of thing I had in mind in connection with university education; that will come under the Department of Pensions and National Health?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The selection of those qualified for vocational ' training will come under the Department of Pensions and National Health. At the present time we are making a national survey of the whole field of education for discharged soldiers, and that survey will be completed in two or three months.

Including university
education?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The regulations in regard to university education are now complete, but the survey is being made in regard to the physical, educational and vocational facilities available in every part of Canada.
Then I shall wait until the minister reaches his estimates.

In view of the fact that the administration of the rehabilitation regulations, including vocational training, comes under the Department of Pensions and National Health, what function is performed by the Department of Labour in connection with the expenditure of this money?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: They are doing the actual work at the present time.
Do I understand that this is before discharge?
No.
I do not see where the work of one department ends and that of the other begins. Perhaps the minister will make that clear.

I can tell my hon,. friend how it happened. We have been conducting these classes for several years now, since they were introduced by the late Mr. Rogers in 1936. When the present situation developed the Department of Labour had the machinery and the experience, and we took over this obligation from pensions and national health, but the setting of the scale of remuneration and the regulations in connection with education are matters for that department. The training in industry and in the technical and vocational schools is undertaken by the Department of Labour.
A short time ago the minister indicated that determination of the date on which actual service began was a matter for the Department of Pensions and National Health.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: That is in the case of a discharged soldier.
Then what about a discharged member of the air force?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: The same thing applies.
That is not decided by the Department of National Defence?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: 1-is decided by the regulations of the service branch in which the man has served, and the Department of Pensions and National Health must take the regulations of that branch.
But pensions and national health have no control over that at. all; it is up to the defence department?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Yes.

Item agreed to.

War Appropriation-Labour
Assistance in meeting extra costs of the universities in accelerating certain courses and to provide loans to certain students, $440,000.

What types of students are given this assistance? Is it given to any young man who finds that he cannot afford to go through university; and if so what procedure should be followed by one desiring to apply for assistance?
It is in medicine, dentistry, science and engineering; those are the four courses; first year engineering and science, and I think they must be over five years in medicine.
And will these amounts be in addition to what the act actually calls for?

These students are
chosen by a committee in each university,, and an allowance of approximately $275 is given the student towards the cost of his education at that particular university. The number of students who have been assisted in this way to date is just over two thousand.
What arrangements are made in connection with the loans, with regard to repayment?
That is undertaken at each university. Some universities give the money, while others lend it. It is all arranged between the federal government, the provincial government and the university.
If it is the money of the federal government, why should the university have the right to say whether it shall be given or lent?
Where it is the money of the federal government it is purely a loan, but this is usually a joint arrangement between the provincial and federal governments. There is nothing new about it.
It is a federal loan to the students, is it?
Yes.
Lent by whom?
In some cases a federal loan and in some cases a joint loan.

But a loan in every
case?
Not in every case; where the province puts it up it may be a gift, at the discretion of the province and the university.
How many provinces are making this a gift, and how many make it a loan, does the minister know?
I do not know. I can say that one good Scotch university, Queen's, makes it a loan.
Some of us would be interested in knowing what is being done in our own provinces. What about Saskatchewan?
I shall get the information for my hon. friend; it is best to be sure about it.

Is the boy given more than a one-year course? My understanding is that if a boy gets this loan he has to sign up for enlistment at the end of the first year of his course. The boy may go on if his standing is high enough and he can finance himself; as long as he remains in the good graces of the universities he may continue his education, but if he gets this loan from the government it is because of the fact that he agrees to go into the army at the end of one year. He can only get a one-year education.

No, he is allowed to
complete his course, but he does not get the loan except under certain stipulations; that is, he either goes into the fighting forces or into some industry, at the direction of the Minister of Labour.

I wish the minister
would look into that more carefully, because I am definite on the point. I could give the names of boys who were given this opportunity definitely on the basis that they could get only a one-year course.

It may be that in the
judgment of the university a young fellow's academic standing was not sufficiently high to permit him to continue his course, but in all these courses they are permitted to complete their education. I wish the hon. member would give me the particulars of the case he has mentioned.
I shall do so.
Is it not true that some of the universities are giving a special one-year course to officer material? Perhaps that is what the hon. member has in mind.
But not under the jurisdiction of my department.
Will the minister obtain the information, and let us have the picture in connection with the various universities?
Yes.

Item agreed to.
War Appropriation-Labour
National war labour board, $468,445.

As I understand it, the national war labour board was reconstituted by order in council P.C. 1141 on February 11 of this year. At the time it was reconstituted three members were appointed to it, namely the Hon. Mr. Justice C. P. McTague, the Hon. J. J. Bench and Mr. J, L. Cohen. First, before the board was set up, Mr. Bench was appointed to the senate, and when I read in the press that he had been appointed to this board I was favourably impressed, because I thought it was an instance of giving to a man in public life a position in which he could do a good piece of work. I was disappointed, however, to find two and a half months later that another order in council was passed providing for the revocation of the appointment of the Hon. Senator J. J. Bench, and the appointment in his place of Mr. Lalande, at a salary of 310,000 a year.
In the second order in council, P.C. 3512, passed on April 29, 1943, we find the following statement:
Whereas the Minister of Labour reports with reference to the war-time wages control order (P.C. 5963 dated July 10, 1942), that the Honourable Senator J. J. Bench, K.C., in accordance with an understanding at the time of his appointment has submitted his resignation as a member of the national war labour board. . . .
What was the understanding at the time of the appointment, and what was the reason for placing on the board a man who would go into the various matters coming before the board, and who would become acquainted with the problems with which the board was confronted, only to have his appointment revoked within two and a half months?
I do not know whether the hon. member knows Senator Bench very well.
I do not know him at all.
He is not strong physically.
He is under forty years of age.
That may be true; but I am sure if my hon. friend knew Senator Bench and the nature of his disability, he would not have made the observations he has made.
What I have said was not said with the intention of casting any reflection at all. I wished only to have an explanation.

Well, that is the explanation. It was understood and discussed. I discussed this matter with Senator Bench, and it 
was understood he would not stay very long. The reason why he left as soon as he did was that he could not stand the strain of the work of the board. He had to go south to recuperate. - Senator Bench felt that, in view of the pressing nature of the cases before the board, it was his duty to resign. That is what he did, and the other gentleman was appointed in his place.
That was in accordance with the understanding; but it was not the understanding that he would quit within two and a half months.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Senator Bench is a close friend of mine. I know the hon. member did not intend to cast any reflection, but since he has made the observations he did make may I say that Senator Bench had been in the armed services, serving as a commissioned officer. He was discharged for reasons of health.
I assure the committee I did not intend any reflection whatsoever.

Item agreed to.
Expenses in connection with general labour transference in war industries and agriculture, $500,000.

I should like to raise a point on this item. To-day we approach the end of June, when schools are closing. On Saturday evening I had a long-distance telephone conversation with the secretary of the teachers' alliance in Alberta. It was drawn to my attention that a large number of teachers are anxious to find war work in the summer. It was pointed out that they had made applications to the selective service branch in Edmonton for wrork suitable to their particular experience, physical conditions and aptitude, but that they were being told in practically all cases that the work available to them would be work on the farms.
Probably some of the younger men and women in the teaching profession are quite able to transfer from the schools to farm work. But a large number of teachers, both male and female, on account of the sedentary type of work they have been doing for ten or fifteen or more years are not physically fit for farm work.
I have a letter confirming the telephone conversation, but shall not take the time of the committee to read it. The point in question is that in Edmonton, or at points just outside Edmonton, there is a good deal of clerical work, such as checking and the like, for which applications are being invited. These teachers, who are probably best fitted

War Appropriation-Labour
in many respects for that kind of work, are told that they cannot have it, often because the employing firm is a United States organization. And yet, as many of us know, numbers of men are being brought in from the United States to do various types of work in northern Alberta. These men are brought in long distances, and at great expense. If people are available locally who, by experience and physical condition, are fitted to do that type of wbrk, it seems to me that they should not be directed to work they cannot do, and that they should be given an opportunity of doing the work for which they are fitted.
This is something to which the department might give its attention. In the next week or ten days, approaching the end of June, a number of teachers will be released from schools all across Canada. I believe the school terms do not resume in some of the provinces until about October 15. That is the position in Alberta; and I believe some of the other western provinces and the province of Ontario are extending the vacation period in the same way. This is being done so that teachers and pupils alike may undertake other types of work.
It is true that the work on the farm must be done and that labour is short. Where people are fitted physically or by experience for that kind 'of work I agree they should be directed to do it. I am not criticizing that at all. But if they are not fitted, then I say they should not be debarred from doing the kind of work for which they are fitted.
Mr. John Barnett, who has written me, tells me that he makes no criticism of the officials of selective service in Edmonton. He points out that in every instance the treatment received by those who made inquiries at the Edmonton office was exceedingly courteous, and that there was no complaint to make in that respect. I mention that only because it might be inferred that there had been some trouble when, in fact, there has been none at all.
I was surprised to hear the minister's announcement in the house that farm labour was to be transferred from Saskatchewan to Ontario at this season of the year. I cannot understand where that source of labour is available; and if it is available I do not understand why it cannot be used in districts in Saskatchewan, Manitoba or Alberta where there has been a shortage of labour. Both in eastern and western Canada, particularly in the east, I think it is more a maldistribution of farm labour. No thorough survey has been made
to ensure that farm labour is directed to those places where it can be utilized most economically and efficiently.
In my opinion the question of labour on our farms will become more acute as the days go by. The demand for food will become greater. Indeed, we are witnessing to-day one of the most surprising shortages of food in the United States. Yesterday I was reading some articles in the New York Times regarding shortages in the United States which are rather alarming. We have a little rationing in our own country, but we are not short of anything particularly. The people overseas are on fairly short rations because the food we are getting to them is not enough. If we open up any part of Europe food will be required in very large quantities. So that it seems to me it is essential that we should keep up our food supply. I had this in mind when I was discussing the whole man-power situation last Friday.
Perhaps there could be a transfer by persuasion of labour from farms where it is not vitally needed to other farms in the same area. I have heard of cases in both this and the neighbouring province where a number of people, old and young, are employed on farms who might be more efficiently employed on different farms or on different types of farms in the same locality. But even if we do this there will still be an insufficient supply of agricultural labour. I wish the minister would take up with his colleagues, particularly the Minister of Munitions and Supply, the question of providing more machinery for the farms. I am thinking not only of the western farms where mechanization has become fairly universal on the larger units, but also of the eastern dairy farms. I know of cases where four or five people with a milking machine are able to handle sixty, seventy or even more head of milch cattle.
