speechtext:
The romance is being
taken out of it.

The minister might take up with his colleagues the question of providing more machinery for the farm. This should be possible if some branches of our war industry have reached their peaks and are now slowing down, especially if they were previously engaged in the manufacture of farm equipment. I ask the minister to give particular consideration to my first question, that teachers who are not particularly equipped to go on the land be permitted to take positions which their physical condition will permit them to fill more efficiently and more in the interests of the country.
War Appropriation-Labour
I think it is fair to say that a large proportion of the teachers in western Canada are children of farmers, and that is where they should go in the holidays.
If they are physically fit.

If they are physically fit. I want to make that very definite because many hon. members have been talking about the shortage of farm labour. These people will have to go where they can be best used. While I cannot give the number of men that will be required on the Alaska highway, I may say that some months ago I discussed this matter with the United States authorities, and the number of men that will be engaged during the summer on this project staggers the imagination. We just have not a man-power pool in western Canada even to attempt to meet this need. Under these conditions our good friends to the south have arranged for a labour supply themselves. We could not disrupt the labour pool in western Canada in order to do this work. My hon. friend can rest assured that the selective service officers will be judicious in their decisions in connection with teachers being sent into agriculture this summer.
My hon. friend referred to the question of a labour supply for the west. My mind goes back to last fall when, on account of weather conditions, we were faced with a difficult situation in western Canada. University students and some farmers were sent to the west. I think it is only in the nature of one good turn deserving another that any men in western Canada who are able to give assistance to farmers in the east between the planting season and threshing should do so. This is required particularly in connection with the hay crop which is heavy this year. We are taking the advice of our organizations in Saskatchewan and other parts of the west as to what men are available.
On the question of organization, I may say that in Saskatchewan we have a "win the war committee" in every municipality. The driving force between these committees is to have labour available where it is most needed, not only in connection with planting the crops but in converting them into food and generally supplying the needs of all year round agriculture. Committees have been established in every parish in Quebec and in every county in Ontario. That is the way we are organizing in order to make the best possible use of the labour supply available.
We must not forget that there are about
770,000	farms in Canada. I think it is fair to say that there is at least one man and woman on every farm. We are apt to be a little confused in our thinking and compare

labour conditions in agriculture prior to 1941 with what they are to-day. I do not think that is a fair comparison to make because in those depression years there were many people on our farms who were living there rather than working. There was no employment for them in the industrial areas. I have seen the figures, and there has never been much more than
60.000	hired men engaged in the farming industry of this country. When these comparisons are made I think due allowance should be made for the point I have raised.
In connection with agricultural machinery I can tell my hon. friend that a committee of the Department of Agriculture is working with the priority committee of my department in connection with the supply of agricultural machinery for the farmers of this dominion. No doubt by the time we get around to the agricultural estimates the Minister of Agriculture will have something to say on this matter.

The point I was making was that no matter what their physical condition might be, the only rvork that has been offered to male teachers in Edmonton has been that of labourer and farm worker, and to the women teachers, that of waitress and laundress. That is what I want the minister to look into, to see if these could not be extended.

My hon. friend will
appreciate that there is a tight situation in Edmonton.

I do not belong to the teaching profession, but during the. past three or four weeks I have had several communications from teachers in my province and I have taken up some of these cases with the Minister of Labour. So far as teachers being sent to the farm is concerned, I support the argument of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. He must have a copy of the notes I have before me because he has discussed the points I intended to raise. When the minister is preparing to send these teachers to the farm he should consider the wages that are to be paid. A farmer cannot pay wages that will be attractive to a teacher and I am afraid it will be found that many of them will be trying to get into other lines of work. I agree with the minister that a number of the teachers have come from the farm, but I suggest that a number of them are not in shape to stand the hard work that must be done on the farm. In regard to the lady teachers, I would like the minister to make it clear whether those who have matrimonial engagements will be compelled to have a stay of proceedings on such engagements until the war is over, or whether

War Appropriation-Labour
they can go ahead, because I know a number who have engagements for next month or immediately after school is out. Would the minister let us know the Liberal policy or definition of these teachers being frozen?
All matters relating to the affections I shall refer to my assistant.

I hope they will be as well taken care of as he has taken care of his own along that line.
The minister in his statement on Wednesday last gave great prominence to the agricultural profession, if I may call it that; I only wish it was elevated to that happy position. As reported at pagff3934 of Hansard, the minister gave agriculture quite a boost. It was a real Liberal boost; it consisted of words only and said nothing about financial compensation. The minister said:
What our farmers have done is to produce more and more with fewer people. This record of achievement by our farmers, their wives, their children, and their hired men and women will be read some day as one of the glorious chapters in our history. I should like as Minister of Labour to pay special tribute to the hired men and women on the farms. They are too often forgotten in plans for social betterment. Their lot is not an easy one or an exciting one. They are doing a grand war job to-day for this nation.
I want to join most heartily with the Minister of Labour in that statement, because he is quite correct in saying that fewer of our people are producing more food than ever before. The one drawback is that they are still not paid for their labours. I do not think that statement can be successfully challenged if we take agriculture as a whole. We have been told time and again that prices of agricultural products cannot be figured out and that for that reason we cannot get parity prices or the cost of production. I would advise the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Agriculture, and even the Minister of Finance, that if they have not sufficient statisticians here in Ottawa, I can get a number of farmers to' work these things out for them if they on their part will then agree to pay the cost of production. We have on the farm a number of accountants, and while they may not be regarded in Ottawa as having very much ability because they are on a farm, nevertheless they can do accounting efficiently. So that if the government cannot find statisticians here in Ottawa, I can give them the names of some people who can work these things out for them.
Farm production, I am afraid, will be a little disappointing to the government this year, even though the Minister of Agriculture told a Liberal convention only a couple of
days ago that everything would be all right unless some hoarding was done. I hope that his predictions will be realized in the interests of agriculture and of our allies.
The shortage of farm machinery has been spoken of by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. I have worried quite a little about this shortage, because I know of dozens of fanners in my part of the country who have put in applications for machinery and have not been able to purchase it. The shortage of good farm machinery will be reflected in farm production this summer and harvest because, if you have a poor binder or some such machine, time will be wasted needlessly, and when I say wasted I mean just that, because with fewer good operators our machinery should be kept up to a very high standard.
Coming now to the extra hours of labour,
I want to say that farmers have worked extra hours ever since I came to Canada, at Least some twenty-nine years ago. Other lines of industry have an eight-hour day with half a day off a week, but twelve to sixteen hours a day is the average day's labour for the .farmer in Canada. If you go on the farm and watch the farmer-I do not care whether it is in eastern Canada or western Canada or the central provinces-you will find that twelve to sixteen hours is the average working day, and with poor compensation for these hours of labour I think the farmers are not being justly treated. Perhaps we farmers will have to do the same as the industrialists did in August, 1939. They said: If we do not get the cost of production plus, we are not going to manufacture. The farmers have not yet come to that point, and I hope it will never be necessary for them to do so, but in case it is, I do not think the country could blame 'the farmer for taking that step to get the cost of production if he cannot get it in any other way. We have a system of just prices for other products, and there is no reason in the world why the farmer should not be treated the same as any other industry.
The call-up of men from the farms is a matter that is particularly under the jurisdiction- of the Minister of Labour. During recent days figures have been given showing the trend away from the farms. I think the time has come and our agriculture production has reached the stage when we must not allow any more of our farmers to be called up. Otherwise the supply of food for the united nations may be drastically reduced, and our armies cannot fight unless we supply them with the food they need.

In 'connection with farm help for the coming harvest, I hope the minister will see to it that we are provided with all the help that will be required for this harvest season. While a lot of benefit was derived from the help that was sent from eastern Canada to western Canada last fall, I do not think the picking of those men was just what it might have been, so that I suggest to the minister that care be taken this year and that preparations be made early to make a better choice of help to send out west for the harvest. I realize that last year it was done in a hurry, and without exception the men who were sent out did the very best they could so far as I know, but a man who comes out of a university and goes straight on the farm to stook or pitch bundles for twelve hours a day is up against a pretty stiff job.

Under this heading I wish to ask the minister for some clarification of the recent order with respect to students of sixteen, seventeen and eighteen years of age, with particular reference to forestry students. I have written a letter to the director about this matter but have not as yet had any reply.
I would point out that in New Brunswick there is one of the few forestry schools in the Dominion of Canada. It has been the practice for the students to take their theory in the academic term; and the pulp and paper companies, and other large timber limits holders, as opportunity permits, make it possible for them to apply the principles and the theories which they learn in the academic course. This year, in accordance with the usual practice, a number of these students of the university of New Brunswick made application to the paper companies in my province for employment, and I may say to the minister that of course the pecuniary reward is a great inducement to these students. Arrangements were made for several-not a great many-to go into the forestry departments of the paper companies and to report for duty on a certain date. Then intervenes the recent order with respect to students, and they are told that before they can be permitted to go they must present a permit from the national selective service local office. On applying for that permit they are refused on the ground of the broad-perhaps I should say, the limited, or not very liberal-interpretation of the regulation. I am not finding any fault with the selective service offices at Fredericton, but these students are told they cannot enter the service of the companies because they must go on farms. These men are not a large class. If it is necessary in New Brunswick that they do so they will

comply with that rigid enforcement of the order, but I suggest to the minister that the regulation be interpreted liberally. These young men are pursuing their studies; at the same time they are earning money by going into these forestry camps and doing the work of forestry students, and I would hope that the minister and his director of national selective service would interpret the rules liberally and allow these young men, who do not want to go on farms and feel they will not receive the pecuniary reward they would obtain in the forestry camps, to proceed as has been the custom in years gone by. These young men in due course will be required to answer the call .for national selective service, and I believe they are patriotic and will be prepared to do so. But they are still under age, and I think that in justice to them they should be allowed to pursue their vocation, preparing themselves in a financial way for the next term's work, and follow the practice of their chosen profession, rather than have to go on farms. I should like the minister to elucidate that position.

The extension of the permit system to take in persons from sixteen to eighteen years of age inclusive is merely an extension of the other system, so that we can have some control over the movements, particularly during the summer months, of people in these age groups. I thank my hon. friend for bringing this question to my attention. As a matter of fact, we have already sent out instructions in conformity with his suggestion.
Thank you.

I think it is sound and logical. The university of New Brunswick has, I suppose, one of the finest forestry courses in North America. I look upon these young men very much as one would regard science students. We make provision for science students to go into industry where they can get experience during the summer vacations, and I think it is logical for young men in this forestry course to go into the lumber industry during the vacations! period of their course. My hon. friend can rest assured that as far as my department is concerned that will be done.
That is most satisfactory.

I should like to refer for a moment to the employment of teachers during the summer holidays. Can the minister tell us what if any provision has been made by his national selective service officers for absorbing some 80,000 teachers who

War Appropriation-Labour
have been released from schools to-day or will be released to-morrow. I know that until last year no provision whatever was made for the absorption of these people into the labour market, and the selective service was absolutely helpless last spring when teachers in any numbers came for guidance. In the Toronto offices the interviewers in the selective service bureaux were given every morning for weeks, by the man in charge, a notice at the beginning of the day saying, "No employment for teachers", in order that the number of teachers coming in and applying for work would not occupy the time of the people in the offices. The same applied to Ottawa and every large centre across the dominion. No assistance was given to these people who desired to procure two or three months' employment. I know that last September, when the classes opened, most of the teachers' federations across the country wrote to selective service officers asking that they begin now, early in the year, to lay some plans whereby that force of help could be used during the summer months. I am surprised to hear that the same complaint has been raised this year as in former years. Can the minister tell us what decision has been made?

A month ago a directive was sent out to the 216 officers of selective service advising them to encourage teachers to register at the offices. In addition to that, a letter went forward to all the provincial departments of education along the same lines, and they in turn, I am informed, wrote to all the school boards in the respective jurisdictions. I am prepared to admit that this time last year our machinery was not as good as it is at the moment, and I am prepared to predict that six months from now it will be a great deal better than it is at the present moment. I am not making apologies to anybody for the work of the officials of selective service. As I said the other evening, this is a new organization; they are working in a virgin field as far as this country is concerned, and I think it can be safely stated without any fear of successful contradiction that as the days go by,' notwithstanding criticisms by people who should know better-and in saying this I am not referring to any hon. member-they have acquitted themselves very well. My hon. friend can rest assured that as far as the teachers are concerned everything that can be done will be done to see that they are channeled into useful occupations in the province of Ontario.

The only answer the minister has given is that some time ago
certain selective service directives were sent out. Has any specific provision been made for absorbing 80,000 teachers whose services will be available for the next three months?

I can only say to my hon. friend that the mechanics are there to take about 80,000 teachers. We apply a policy, wre send out the directives, and then the organization of course undertakes the carrying out of those directives. It is a physical impossibility for me to know, for instance, all the vacancies that occur from day to day in my hon. friend's own community in the city of Toronto; but from what I see in this community I do not think anybody will have a great deal of difficulty in getting employment for three months this summer. I believe that, with the assistance of our selective service organization, and subject of course to the exceptions which occasionally occur to every rule, any schoolteacher who wants a job this summer will be able to get it.
The minister said something about laying down a policy.
The employment officers were told to get a list of vacancies and to direct teachers into them when school broke up.

When was that
information sent out?

A month ago. In connection with farming, there is, I submit, evidence that we have done some planning in the Department of Labour, when one considers the progressive steps that we have taken during the last six or eight months. I am not looking for credit for the Department of Labour, but it indicates that last winter we were alive to the situation that would develop this spring, and plans have already been made for the harvest this fall, at least to face up to the harvest in the west.
Is it the understanding, then, that the directions sent out give a broader interpretation than is given at Edmonton?
Yes. But do not try to get me in a corner on this. I want to have some leeway for my people in the country.
That is what I am trying to do.
I know you are trying to do it, but you are not going to. Getting back to Alberta, apart from the Alcan-	*

Alaska, not Alcan. That is a hideous name.
War Appropriation-Labour
Commons

Apart from the Alaska highway, then-I know why people want to work on the highway; it is to make money- the priority list that exists in the Ottawa office of the selective service must be the yardstick for the guidance of the officials in charge there in the placement of teachers.

We have had some experience in the past in putting people to work on farms. Last year, when the harvest was on, a great many people from eastern Canada went to the farms and the arrangement was not satisfactory. Now we are trying to do the same thing with teachers. Last fall we had evidence to show that the people who went out there from eastern Canada, though they were enthusiastic and tried to do their best, did not come up to the required standard for farm labour. They failed for two reasons: first, they were not experienced, and, second, they were not in a physical condition to carry on. I do not care whether a teacher has been raised on a farm, if he has been teaching for a number of years he is not in a condition to go and work on a farm. There is another aspect to this matter. I believe that the majority of teachers, with their education and the extra knowledge they have as compared with ordinary labourers, could be used more beneficially in some other line of industry than on farms. It might be possible to put teachers in clerical positions in offices where such work is necessary and better results would be obtained than by some teachers being put on farms, because they would not be in a position to carry on.
We have a wrong idea about farm work. Those who think anyone can go and work on a farm are definitely wrong. It takes four weeks at least for one to get hardened if one is to carry on even then. In my opinion, the government would simply waste a lot of time by putting teachers on farms. Apparently the Minister of Labour has taken the attitude that they will go on the farms or not work at all. There are many teachers who will not work on the farm, and if they are forced to go on the farm they will not work at all. Whether that is patriotic or not, that is what will happen in many instances.
Another question to be considered is that of salary. A teacher who is used to a good salary and is forced to go on the farm will be dissatisfied, because a large number of people have left farms on account of the inadequacy of the remuneration paid, and the government is goisg to replace those people with teachers who will receive a low income. The farmers cannot afford to pay more than they are paying; but on the other hand this will prevent
TMr. MacNicol.]
teachers from taking up any other type of work in which they would receive a higher income.
These difficulties are all before us, and the minister would do well to look into the matter thoroughly before attempting to force teachers into occupations which they may not care for or for which they are not fitted. I join in the other remarks that have been made with regard to teachers.

A great deal has been said about getting workers for the farms, but another aspect that must be kept in mind, is that of retaining men on the farms. I believe the selective service should go farther than they have gone in that direction. Anyone acquainted with agricultural conditions knows that the farmers very often hire men during the temporarily slack season in order to have them during the busy season, and under present selective service regulations farm help must give seven days' notice before leaving, and that at a busy time. That is a serious element in the agricultural farm labour requirements. I believe the government would be well advised to take the matter up on a cooperative basis with the provincial legislature with a view to having a little more compulsion on the farm hand, compelling him to remain with the farmer during the busy season, instead of being lured to some other farmer or some other industry or occupation by virtue of higher wages and other inducements such as easier hours and so on. If you look at our provincial statutes dealing with wages, failure to pay wages and so on, you will find that a heavy penalty is imposed upon the employer who does not pay his employee the wages contracted for. Selective service could assist agriculture quite well if they would specialize and pay more attention to compelling the farm labourer to render the services for which he has contracted. In that regard it will be necessary to take the matter up with the provincial legislature from the point of view of jurisdiction.
I have heard complaints over this very question, where farmers, having hired men, lose them. True, there is a law that the man must give seven days' notice but there is not enough sting to compel compliance with the regulations, nor is there enough power exercised by the selective service to keep a man at his job, to which he is so essential.

It is wonderful how the discussion develops. I have been sitting here for quite a while, and I have heard many different matters discussed under this item. Together with the other hon. members I was certainly glad to hear the minister, as reported at

War Appropriation-Labour
page 4019 of Hansard for June 23, pay a compliment to the farmers for what they have done, and I certainly agree with what he said.
I am interested in the transfer of men from western Canada to the east to help out the farmers in this part of the country, and I am anxious that those men will get back to the west in time to do the work there. I think they will do a much better job in the east than was done in the west by some of the young fellows who went from our universities to help -with the harvest last fall, and I am anxious to see that they all get back to where they will be needed at harvest time. It has been suggested already that the department should make plans well in advance to see that adequate help is provided for the coming harvest, and I think it is important that these things be organized in plenty of time.
With respect to these selective service offices to which the minister has referred so often, while out of the city on Saturday I had a little chat with a gentleman who has something to do with employing men for a certain organization which has a number of offices across Canada. He told me some of the difficulties they' are meeting in securing men through these selective service offices; he mentioned the bottlenecks, the difficulties that arise through the red tape and routine that must be followed. He told me that it took from four to five days to get anyone after his firm made application to one of these offices. He mentioned the number of applications and forms that had to be filled out, and I think the whole thing could be made very much simpler if proper men were placed in charge, for I believe many people are being placed in the selective service offices who do not know their business.
Coming back to the teachers, I believe many of them in western Canada will be ready to take employment during the vacation, and I think they should, be allowed to accept employment in the districts in which they have been teaching. I believe they will do good work. I venture to suggest that many of them will be able to give better service than many members of this house will be able to give if we are kept here much longer. In conclusion, I repeat that I hope these men coming from the west to work on the farms of eastern Canada will be sent back when their work here is over, and will not be frozen to jobs in the east.

Is there a shortage of labour in Saskatchewan at the present time, as the records of the department would indicate? The minister mentioned that he had
victory committees operating in all districts. What do their reports show as to whether there is a shortage of labour?

My hon. friend will
appreciate that we have no reports from individual committees, but we have a general report and the condition is much better than they expected it to be.
But there is still a shortage?
No, we expect to move a thousand farm labourers east from Saskatchewan.
There will be a shortage? Mr. MITCHELL: For harvest?
How many men have you taken off the farms, through selective service, say up to the end of June?
You mean to come to eastern Canada?
No; through selective service; men called into the army.
None.
Well, there are calls going throughout Saskatchewan for men to report. -
That is merely to report for medical examination; that is not a call for the army.
No men are being taken off the farms at the present time?
No.
What wages are being paid the men who are being brought east from Saskatchewan?

They are getting the
going rate in the district, whatever it is.

What is it at the
present time?
It varies, I suppose from $40 a month to $75 a month, and we pay the return fare.
You are paying everything?

Yes, everything except $5. I think the return fare comes to $120, and we pay it all but S5 in order to make sure that they go back again.
Progress reported.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext: The house resumed consideration in committee of a resolution to grant to his majesty certain sums of money for the carrying out of measures consequent upon the existence of a state of war-Mr. Usley-Mr. Donnelly in the chair.
National selective service programme, $8,680,225.

Mr. Chairman, on
account of a misunderstanding of the statistical tables on mobilization as appearing in Hansard at page 3954, I should like to make a statement for the information of the committee. At this time the regulations apply to men born in any of the years 1902 to 1916 inclusive, who on July 15, 1940, were unmarried or widowers without child or children, or who have since that date been divorced or become judicially separated, or widowers without child or children, and to all men born in any of the years 1917 to 1924 inclusive, except that men born in the year 1924 are not ordered out for medical examination until they have reached the age of nineteen years. Within fourteen days of the date appearing on the order for medical examination, a man may apply in writing to his registrar for postponement of his military training.
Applications for postponement will come under three main headings: (1) men essential in agricultural operations; (2) men essential in war industry and essential industry, public utilities and so on, and (3) men whose departure for military training would cause extreme hardships to their dependents.
Mobilization boards hear applications for postponements, and decisions of boards are final. Boards may, however, of their own motion, reconsider applications for postponement. Representatives of agriculture and representatives of national selective service, civilian section, as well as representatives of the Department of National Defence may attend and make representations at meetings of mobilization boards.
Under national selective service mobilization regulations bona fide students of colleges and universities taking certain specified courses are allowed to pursue their course of studies undisturbed, provided that, if medically fit, they take the military training prescribed, and also pass their scholastic examinations.
War Appropriation-Labour

Non-declarant enemy aliens as well as neutral aliens who forgo naturalization fights are accepted under these regulations. Men who have been granted a postponement are ordered out for military training immediately following expiration of the postponement, unless further application is made and granted.
Men ordered to report for training are supplied with transportation, lodging and subsistence warrants as required. Upon reporting at district depots or military training centres of the Department of National Defence (army), men are again medically examined by medical officers of the Department of National Defence, and, if found fit, are taken on strefigth and enrolled. As of that time they cease to be under the jurisdiction of the Department of Labour.
That is my point. Many hon. members come to me and speak with respect to men who are already in the army. Of course, once they are in the army they cease to be under the jurisdiction of the Department of Labour, and come under the jurisdiction of the Minister of National Defence.
Men rejected upon reporting at district depots of training centres for medical reasons are returned home and are provided with transportation, subsistence and lodging warrants. A medical officer is attached to each of the thirteen districts or divisions. His duties are to scrutinize carefully all medical examinations and certificate forms completed by examining physicians and to advise the registrar on matters of a medical character. Certificates of medical examination have been issued to men who, on account of their physical condition, are not required to report for the time being.
Medical revision boards have been set up at a number of points in Canada under the Department of National Defence where men who are placed in medical categories other than those at present acceptable by the military authorities are being medically reexamined. As I have told the committee, men subject to national selective service mobilization regulations whose conscientious objection to bearing arms is recognized by national selective service are called out for alternative service work of a civilian character for the duration of the war. Steps are being taken to mobilize these conscientious objectors for work in agriculture and in other private essential industry. I went into this more at length when I made my initial presentation to the committee the other day.
Under part II of the regulations, men who are not fit for .military training but who are

otherwise fit for special duty with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police may be ordered out for special duty at the request of the Minister of Justice. These men may apply for postponement on the same grounds and in the same manner as men ordered out for *military training. Divisional registrars have been hampered in their work because so. many have failed to report changed addresses. Sometimes we are critical of the man on the street for not complying with the regulations with respect to change of address, but may I suggest to hon. members that they look at their own registration cards and see if they have complied with the regulations. After having done that, perhaps they will be a little more charitable.
Is a member supposed to change his address?
A member of the House of Commons comes within the law just the same as the man on the street.
He does not have to give Ottawa as his new address.
Is a member supposed to change his address from that of his riding?

Oh, no, that is elementary. During the year ended March 31, 1943, the number of address changes notified to national registration authorities was 779,278, or over 60,000 a month. Hon. members will appreciate the amount of detailed organization work that that entails in itself, without the other ramifications of administration which are encountered in the national selective service organization. The problem of tracing these men has been partly solved by the compulsory re-registration of men who have not received their order-medical examination. Preferred attention is being given to the prosecution of delinquents. The reexamination by the army medical boards of 150,000 men, being done on the recommendation of the medical advisers, is nearly completed. Approximately thirty-five per cent of the men reexamined have been found to be in acceptable categories to be ordered out for military training. Transportation, subsistence and lodging warrants are being issued to these men.
While most designated age classes are being ordered to have their medical examinations, the volume of work of the mobilization section of the national selective service will nevertheless continue in view of the fact that mobilization is at the mopping-up stage, so

War Appropriation-Labour
to speak, which must be carried out for the purpose of bringing into the armed forces all the men liable to compulsory mobilization.
As to the method of call-up, may I say that in making requisitions, the Department of National Defence state the total number required and allot them to districts in accordance with their training facilities. This determines where the men report, but does not determine where they come from. These allotments are sent on to the registrar as a matter of convenience. If any division were able to mobilize more men than the Department of National Defence could train at that point, they -would be sent to other training centres. That is somewhat of a change from the previous procedure. The number of men called out in a district or division is determined by the application of the mobilization regulations. Every man in a designated class, fit for military service, who is subject to the regulations is selected for the armed forces unless he receives postponement on any of the grounds set out in the regulations, such as essential industry, farming, national interest, compassionate grounds or conscientious objection. It may be interesting to the committee to know what is done in New Zealand, and I quote from a statement made by the minister of man-power of that country in connection with the man-power regulations. He said:
They are to be administered with temperateness and discretion, and will not unduly affect the good -worker or the good employer. The penalties are designed for the malingerer and the defaulter. It is my intention that such a person should be dealt with firmly-
That is the exact position taken by my department.
-on the other hand, where any individual shows .a genuine desire to meet his difficulties squarely these regulations will be so administered as to give him every possible assistance and cooperation. Although regulations are necessary to secure uniformity of practice and in order to harness and coordinate the war effort, it is to cooperation that we must look for good results.
The directions to our Canadian registrars are to deal with every man in the designated class as rapidly as possible. The divisions vary in size. Some have greater difficulty in getting accommodation and staff, and therefore the speed of selection varies, but, in the end, the same result is sought for; that is, all men fit for service in the designated class who are not given postponement and have not volunteered for service in the armed forces, are selected.
The staff concerned with compulsory mobilisation has been increased since the 1st of August, 1942, by 1,575 new employees. These new employees have been engaged for the local divisions, and the total strength of the
staff throughout Canada, including headquarters at Ottawa, is, at the present time, 1,843. This will give some indication to the committee of what I might term the resoluteness of the Department of Labour, and previously the Department of National War Services, in moving in the direction of mobilization of men for the armed forces since last August.
Since December 1, when administrative responsibility with respect to mobilization was transferred to the Minister of Labour, the following procedures have been adopted to enforce the regulations. Compulsory mobilization under the regulations had been enforced against the great majority of those men in the designated classes. Therefore, before proceeding with the compulsory mobilization of men married before July 15, 1940, it was decided to make every effort to complete enforcement against those men who had failed to register in national registration, 1940, or to advise appropriate authorities as to subsequent change of address and other necessary facts.
Accordingly, the mobilization regulations were amended to require the re-registration of men in the then designated age classes who had not been served with notice or order-medical examination. Mobilization registrars were provided with copies of. each re-registration, and instructions were given for the registrars to proceed immediately with the compulsory mobilization of these re-registered men. The registrars were told that it was their primary duty to see to the prompt mobilization of these men. At the present time, the great majority of these re-registered men have been dealt with.
Shortly after December 1, 1942, administrative action was taken for the issuance of certificates to men in designated age classes to indicate compliance with mobilization regulations.
This action constituted the issuance in all appropriate cases of postponement order certificates, medical unfitness certificates, and other certificates indicating compliance with the mobilization regulations. The issuance of these certificates of compliance is practically up to date at present in all of the thirteen offices of the mobilization registrars.
After inspection of the offices of the thirteen mobilization registrars, it was found that registrars were not in possession of a complete up-to-date set of national registration records pertaining to all men in the then designated classes who were residing in the respective administrative divisions of the registrars concerned.

When was that discovered? After December 1 last?
War Appropriation-Labour

I think that is probably right. I must be fair to the previous administration. It must be remembered that for the first two years of the war we had an unemployment problem and we found the recruiting and mobilization of men comparatively easy. I will put it in this way: In those days we were going with the stream, but at the moment we are digging in the cement, which is a much more difficult administrative problem than recruiting men when there was a surplus of man-power. I think some hon. members may have been forgetting the background of this war. In the early days of the war it was a war of position and blockade. We thought we could defeat the enemy through the instrumentality of the Maginot line and the British navy. Personally I always felt that was the wrong approach. But with the fall of France an entirely different problem confronted this dominion. I have some knowledge as all hon. members have of those desperate days when in North America we had hardly enough equipment-I am giving my personal opinion-to defend New York city, let alone the North American continent; and after Dunkirk we had little more left than our bare fists to fight with. I know something of the trials and tribulations of the government in those days. I know it is the easiest thing in the world to back the winning horse after the race has been won. But looking back upon those days I recall some of the sleepless nights I myself spent as an adviser. The people of this country and this government, I think, measured up in a big way to that very difficult situation.
What does the minister mean by digging in the cement? Does he mean that all the volunteers are gone?

I would not say that
altogether.

Pretty
nearly.

I would not say that
altogether. When I speak of digging in the cement I mean we have pretty nearly reached the bottom of the keg.

Not by
the minister's own figures.

I will come to that
in a minute.
Bottom of the barrel.

I like the "bottom of
the keg" myself. I was in the British navy and we used to think more of the keg.

This situation arose because many men had enlisted or changed their address without notifying either the national registration bureau or the mobilization registrar.
However, immediate increased coordination was effected between the national registration bureau and the thirteen offices of the mobilization registrars. The result was that registrars commenced immediately to use the facilities of the national registration bureau in Ottawa for further information in connection with the tracing of men.
It was found that considerable time was required to effect compulsory mobilization of those re-registered in the designated classes. Also time was required to complete the issuance of certificates as to compliance. Therefore, it was not until the middle of April last that an order was issued under the national selective service civilian regulations requiring selective service officers to check as to-non-contravention of the mobilization regulations in all cases of men seeking permits for employment.
Provision was also made under the national selective service civilian regulations affecting men designated for compulsory mobilization, whereby these men are ordered to report at the national selective service local offices when occupied in work of low labour priority, to the end that such men may be transferred to work of high labour priority.
When such men report for compulsory transfer, the selective service authorities check in cooperation with the mobilization registrars to determine as to compliance or non-compliance with the mobilization regulations.
There is in the Department of Labour a branch known as the mobilization survey division. The officials of this branch are responsible for surveying industry, so that designated physically fit men may be withdrawn for the armed forces in an orderly manner.
That is the way in which it is done in Great Britain. They do not merely take the employer's word for it or the employee's, but they have a corps of what they call industrial engineers who go through the various industries.
The department has?

Yes. Since my return
from Great Britain last fall we have adopted a similar policy here. We do not simply take the employer's word for it or the statement of the mobilization board or the employee's word. We have a number of people

War Appropriation-Labour
at the present moment going through the various industries in Canada to squeeze out the men who are suitable for military service.
Are they all practical men?
So far as possible, yes. But when you talk of practical men, that is a matter of opinion.
I mean practical men who know what they see, not office men.

This means that in a specific industry the man-power is graded from skilled to unskilled and, at the same time, a record is made of the physical fitness of the men concerned.
It is the intention by means of these surveys to place the mobilization boards in possession of information respecting the supply of labour available, the importance of the industry to the national economy and the prosecution of the war, and also the importance of the employee's position in the industry.
It is expected that by enforcing the compulsory transfer of unfit men through the facilities in the national selective service local offices an adequate stream of replacements will be provided for those workers withdrawn to meet the needs of the armed forces. To date it has been found that these surveys have revealed already the whereabouts of certain men not in good standing under the regulations.
What does the department do to make sure that men of the proper type are sent to the factories to replace those taken out?
That is done through selective service. You draw men out at one end and push them in at the other. My hon. friend laughs at that.

I was laughing at the
minister's expression.
I think it is a pretty good expression. Men are pushed from the non-essential into the essential industries, and men are drawn out to go into the army.
Suppose a company asks selective service to send them ten boilermakers or ten machinists or ten fitters; how does selective service go about picking the right men?
Selective service offices have information on all the people in the community as to their various skills and training.
Do they insist on a medical examination?

I would not say so. We have bumped into that in connection with coal mining to a limited degree. I think there is some argument for the coal miners in that regard. There may be many coal miners-I do not know that there are-who have left the industry on account of their health; and where men claim that they are not physically able to return to the industry, we are not taking their word for it but are making provision for their medical examination.
At the outset the mobilization regulations provided that upon conviction of a man for non-compliance with order-medical examination or order-military training, it was permissible for the person acting on behalf of the crown to recommend that the court order the convicted person to be escorted in police custody to an appropriate place, for compliance with order-medical examination, or order-military training.
In how many cases did that happen?
I will look up that figure. I would not care to give the number offhand.
Not many yet.

It has begun to show itself. May I mention why I am following my notes closely? I spent all day yesterday with my people on this question, because I thought by this means I could get the explanation over in twenty or twenty-five minutes, whereas it might take much longer if I were to speak extemporaneously or hon. members asked questions across the floor.
It was soon realized that this measure was a desirable one for facilitating enforcement and, therefore, the regulations were further amended to provide that in connection with two other offences, the convicted person could be escorted in police custody to an appropriate place for military training. These offences are: noncompliance with regulations which required reregistration before March 15, 1943, of certain designated men not served with notice or order-medical examination, and non-compliance with the provisions in the regulations as to giving notice of change of address and particulars as to where mail will reach a designated man.
The Royal Canadian Mounted Police report that these more stringent enforcement measures are of great assistance in enforcing mobilization regulations.
War Appropriation-Labour

It is the policy of the administration to reduce as much as possible the work performed by the police authorities in tracing men in cases of mobilization orders undelivered or in cases of non-compliance for other reasons. Registrars have been instructed to take the following steps in the order indicated:
Dispatch of a postcard attached to each mobilization order in question for completion by the delivering postal employee to obtain a report explaining non-delivery or non-compliance.
When did that start?
It started since December 1.
Oh, yes, the other day, long after December 1.

I think my hon. friend will agree with me on this, that as you find these problems you set in motion machinery to meet them. I tell the committee frankly that the labour department is not all-wise; we have not-

If the
minister wants to be frank he will give us the date when that was put into operation.
I shall be glad to do so.
Last week, I think, likely.
I will get the date for my hon. friend.
Will the minister give us an estimate of by what number the staff of the selective service offices will have to be increased to provide for all these regulations and see that everything is working?
I am informed that it was in effect before I took over the mobilization.
I have not heard of it before.

Then, the dispatch of an inquiry to the assistant chief registrar in Ottawa to obtain all available particulars shown on the master card in the national registration bureau or on the records of the three armed forces in Ottawa as of the date of the inquiry; also dispatch of a request for investigation and report to the appropriate police authorities.
On the basis of the facts disclosed by the foregoing procedure, prosecutions are instituted by instructions from registrars to appropriate authorities.

And now let me give the committee some figures to clarify the present position: As at May 15, 1943, the inventory of men in the designated classes is as follows:
Men in designated classes as at 1940: Registration total 1,043,163 less those in course of being called (54,688), net	 988,475
That is the man-power pool.

In the
designated classes.

In the pool.
Men now in armed forces who came out
of foregoing pool	 550,692
Men now on postponement	 100,973
Men unfit	 257,103
Men in C.O.T.C. and	auxiliary units... 5,776
Statutory exceptions (firemen, policemen, clergymen, judges, enemy aliens) 6,257 Residue of original man-power pool unclassified	 67,674
988,475
The last category of which I spoke consists-of men in institutional care and custody, merchant seamen, men in remote areas, duplications and errors in the 1940 registration, men dead, not located on account of unnotified change of address, and delinquents.
The total number unaccounted for, namely 67,674, constitutes 6^ per cent of the manpower pool, and in my opinion this is a credit to the men of Canada.
Hon. members will realize in connection with the statement which I have just made, that in the early days of the mobilization offices-the registrars were not instructed that specific figures would be required at various times, and this fact, together with the tremendous volume of work they had to undertake, created a situation wherein steps had to be taken to obtain an accurate accounting.
The national war services department realized this situation, and arrangements were made to have an actual man-power accounting undertaken which would show the exact classification of every man in the designated classes. This work was commenced last autumn and is not yet completed, but it is anticipated that it will be completed in the course of the next month or so.
I want to thank hon. members for their forbearance in respect of this lengthy detailed explanation, which I thought was necessary so that they could approach this item on the agenda with that critical sense of duty which I know they will apply to it.

The minister tonight, in the early part of his statement,, gave an analysis of the regulations and the modus operandi under which his department-

War Appropriation-Labour *
operates. I assume that when he took over on the 1st of December he found a more or less chaotic condition; in fact, I am quite sure that he did. Some of the admissions which he has made here would indicate that. I think it is fair to say that, ever since the mobilization act was introduced in the early summer of 1940, the man-power problem qua the army-and that is the only phase of this problem with whirfi I propose to deal, and to deal very briefly, this evening-has been one of trial and error, hit or miss, and mostly miss.
The first thing we had was the national registration; and I think it must be apparent to everybody that thousands upon thousands of people in this country-young men in the military ages-did not register. I think we have had a tacit admission from the department that that was the situation, because they had a re-registration and an amnesty against those who did not obey the law. I have forgotten how many the minister said-

One hundred and forty
thousand.

I thought it was around
150,000	who had failed to register. That was an astonishing state of affairs, an astonishing lack of obedience to the law on the part of a substantial number of our citizenship, at a time when Canada was at war, and at a time when the war was in its darkest phases; that is, the year succeeding Dunkirk. I think everyone will agree with ' that. But because of a policy of appeasement, because of the lack of a realistic man-power policy on the part of the administration, that sort of thing was tolerated in this country for months and months and months. And if we have a man-power policy to-day, I suggest to the minister and to the membership of this house that it is a policy which has been improvised from day to day and from month to month as time has gone on. I think that is a fairly correct way of stating the evolution, if I may use that term to describe the man-power policy with regard not only to supplying man-power for the armed forces but to supplying man-power for agriculture and other industry.
I want to be reasonably fair about this. There is, I think, some excuse for improvisation in the early part of the war, because it is a well-known fact that Canada did not set herself manfully to this war for nine months after the declaration of war. We were having what people called a phony war, and did not approach the situation realistically. The cause for that is not far to trace. The
cause for that lies at the door of the administration, which was to have only a reasonable participation in the war. If you want any evidence in substantiation of that assertion, let me page the speeches of the former Minister of Public Works; let me call to mind the speeches of hon. members from the province of Quebec, who have told this house and the country what responsible ministers of the crown told the electors prior to the last election.
And the member for Laval-Two Mountains (Mr. Lacombe).

I would
not page the hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains. I would rather have a higher authority than him.
The late Minister of Justice.

I will come closer home to my hon. friends on the left. I am not unmindful of the declaration made in this house on September 9 by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) in which he laid down four statements, the third of which was that under no consideration should there be an expeditionary force. I pause here to say that never at any time has that third proposition laid down by the socialist party in this country been repudiated by them, either in this house or out of it. So far as I am concerned, they shall never be allowed to get away from that proposition, and they ought never to be allowed to get away from it.

The hon. member will not
have much to do with it.

Maybe I
will not. I shall be one single voice, but in so far as I have power and authority to raise my voice I intend to tell the people of Canada what was the position of hon. gentlemen to my left at the beginning of this war, a position that has never been repudiated by them.
They will not listen to him anyway.

There will be some people who will listen to me. I am satisfied that there will be many who will listen to me as they are listening to me in this house today. There are members of this house who know that I state, generally speaking, the exact truth, and it will not do for the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, with a group of by-elections in sight, to come out now as he
War Appropriation-Labour

did on Friday afternoon last, to try to put his party right with the loyal, patriotic people of Canada.
With respect to one feature of the speech of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, I am in hearty agreement. He said that when the testing time comes; when the casualty lists begin to roll in; when there is brought home to the people of Canada the necessity for reinforcement upon reinforcement, and when the government to whom Providence has been, shall I say, unduly kind during the past three years, is obliged to bring in, as it will be obliged to bring in, the full implementation of the mobilization act as amended' at the last session of parliament, then the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) is going to come to this house and ask for a vote of confidence in a policy which he refused to put into effect at the time when it ought to have been put into effect so that we would have trained reinforcements for our armed forces overseas.
If that is to be a blanket vote of confidence in the administration, they will not get my vote.
Why have you voted for it?

I have not voted for it. I voted for a half-measure because I knew I could not get anything better from this government, and I voted to relieve the government of its pledge to the people. My friends did not vote for that. Why? It is as plain as the nose on your face. They voted as they did because they thought they might curry favour with some sections of the country who did not want total war. I do not think there is the slightest doubt about it. But I did not rise to say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: You said it.

Hon.
gentlemen seem to take umbrage at what I have been saying. Well, let their guilty consciences answer them. That is the best thing I can say to them. Let them search their hearts and minds and consciences as to their course with regard to this gigantic, global struggle and Canada's participation in it. The people will judge if the people know.
Coming back to this question of the mobilization of man-power for the army, I listened with the greatest care to the minister's presentation on Wednesday last, a presentation which I suggest took him and his whole staff three long weeks to make, a studied piece of special pleading to make the worse appear the better cause. That is what the minister's

statement was, an attempt to make the people of Canada believe that all was well. That has been the studied policy of this government in every phase of its war effort since we entered the war in September, 1939-that all was well ; that all is now well, with the mobilization plans of this government. I am going to pay this minister the compliment of saying that until he got into office as the head of the department charged with responsibility for the direction of national service there never was anything but chaos under the former Minister of National War Services and his deputy minister, who now sits in this house as a minister. There never was any real policy of selective service for the army or anybody else. It was catch as catch can with the three armed services, and agriculture took, the hindmost, while industry protected itself as far as it could.
Equality of service! Why, the minister knows in his heart, and it is indicated by the figures he has given here and the figures that have been placed on record as a result of the research of hon. members on this side, chiefly the hon. member for Lake Centre, that some parts of Canada have done twice what other parts have done in regard to national service qua the army. I have a question on the order paper now in regard to the air force, which I believe the minister will answer very shortly. I already have the information, which the minister was good enough to give me privately, but because I do not feel that I should use the figures until they become official I am not going to quote them to-night. I have them right here, however, and I can tell hon. gentlemen that having regard to population in the nine provinces of this dominion there has been no equality of voluntary sacrifice as far as the air force is concerned. When hon. members get the figures for Ontario with reference to voluntary enlistments in the air force and compare them with the figures for the province of Quebec they will be shocked, having regard to the population. That is all I am going to say about that. I shall not give the figures which were given to me by the minister until he answers the question which I placed upon the order paper to-day. The minister will give the figures, and hon. gentlemen then may judge whether or not the statements I have made to-night are correct.
When will the figures be brought down?

That is up to the minister. I have asked the question, as it was suggested I should do, and I have no doubt he will bring down the information. Perhaps it will be brought down to-morrow;

War Appropriation-Labour
at any rate I hope it will be brought down before this debate is over. The minister indicated that if I asked the question he would bring down the information promptly, and I am taking him at his word, but until he does bring down that information I am not going to use the figures he has given me.
In the closing part of his remarks this evening the minister made a statement which greatly intrigued me, because in the analysis he gave he attempted to indicate how the man-power pool has been used up. He did not give us that information last Wednesday; and I want to tell the minister that the figures he gave on Wednesday last indicate that there are half a million men unaccounted for. If those figures are true, it is a national disgrace to Canada. I cannot assert that to-night because I have not been able to follow the figures the minister gave us, I suppose in anticipation of this debate and perhaps an effort to forestall criticism and what may result from it. Therefore I shall reserve some of the things I have to say until I have had an opportunity to analyse the figures the minister gave to-night.
I should like to impress upon the membership of this house the anxiety I feel to-night, and which I have felt through the years since the mobilization act was put into effect, with respect to the number of reinforcements for our troops overseas. We have a volunteer army overseas, composed of so many army corps, so many ancillary forces-I am not so much concerned about that-army headquarters and so on, all going to make up the large number of men indicated by the minister to-night. In that group of men overseas we are supposed to have a number of reinforcement units. How many of those units we have is a dark secret of the military authorities. They absolutely refuse to say. I asked ten pertinent questions of the Minister of National Defence last February. The vital questions remain unanswered to-day, and the minister refuses to answer them; that is, questions having to do with the ratio of reinforcements for our armed forces overseas. The non-essential questions were answered; the vital ones were not, I challenge anyone on the government benches to say that to-day we have that ratio of reinforcements we ought to have if the Canadian army is to go into action soon, as everyone believes it will. I challenge anyone to say that we have a ratio of 100 per cent of reinforcements for the men who are likely to become casualties. I doubt if we have half that; yet I tell the minister and the membership of the government that anything less than 100 per cent of reinforcements, trained men on the ground, ready to
go into their units when the testing time comes, will not be good enough to sustain the position of the Canadian army. That is the anxiety I have, and it has never been allayed by any authoritative figures from the ministry of national defence. They absolutely refuse to divulge this information, though not on the ground that it would be of aid and comfort to the enemy. Not at all; that has never been urged as the reason. They refuse to divulge these figures, and I have the right to form my own opinion as to the reason. My interpretation is that they have not enough and they are ashamed to say so, because if they have not enough I think it is their bounden duty, as the government of this country in a time of war, to get the men, and they have full authority to do so. That is the position.
What did the figures given by the minister the other day indicate? I want to analyse them briefly, and then I am done. The minister revealed that the call-up notices sent out had numbered 988,475; I believe that is his exact figure. At the same time the minister indicated that as a result of these call-up notices some 60S.642 men reported for medical examination. So that at that time there remained unaccounted for some 379,833 men, and there was no explanation given on Wednesday such as has been conjured up here to-night. I am going to help out the minister. Owing to faulty bookkeeping; owing to a lack of liaison between the recruiting offices and the office of national war services, as it was then, undoubtedly a substantial number of men who received these calls volunteered for service, were included in the active army, and became unaccounted for in so far as these figures go. Undoubtedly the reports which should have been made by the recruiting division of the national defence department were not made to the national war services department, or, if they were made, they lagged dreadfully. How many were included in that category I cannot say; I assume perhaps there were
50.000	or more, but that is a long way from 379,833.
There was a method by which each of these men could have been accounted for. There is an official in the Department of National Defence called the director of records, and I do not suppose there is any harder worked officer in the department than this same official. Exact records are kept of every man who has enlisted. When a man enlists voluntarily his papers go to the district office of the director. I happen to know the official in charge of that duty in New Brunswick, and he is as thorough and as exact as would be a chartered accountant. It takes a little time.

War Appropriation-Labour

Then those figures are passed along to the head office in Ottawa. They are all collated, and every man is given a ledger, or a dossier, or whatever one would call it. And there was available at all times to the national war services department the good offices of the director of records here in Ottawa, or of the district recorders-for want of a better term- in the military districts.
I am told there was an absolute lack of liaison on the part of the army, the recruiting division of the army, the recording division of the army and the Department of National War Services. Then, undoubtedly there have been some deaths. Yes, undoubtedly there are some deaths, and the minister is entitled to the benefit of that number. How many? Nobody knows. There is no record of it.
In connection with notices, I think if the minister would be candid with us, and if he would tell us what has actually happened, as revealed in a survey which his department ought to have made, if indeed it has not made it, he would admit that there is case after case after case where certain officials of the government of Canada have deliberately not delivered the notices, or have reported that the men had gone away. I have heard of a case where a postmaster had reported a man was deceased or a man had gone away. That is one reason why some of these notices were not delivered. I wonder how much of a check-up was ever made.
If the hon. member has knowledge of a case of that kind I should like to know about it.
I have heard of it.
I should like to know about it. I have heard of it, too, but I do not know about it.
Then it is the minister's duty to find out. If a report like that is given to the minister, it is his duty to have it checked. It is not my duty.
I would ask my hon. friend-

I am pointing out the possibility of such things. But the fact remains that according to the minister's own figures there was a huge discrepancy of 379,833. I have tried to help the minister out by giving some explanations. I want to say further on that point that because there was a lack of liaison between the recruiting officers of the Department of National Defence and of the naval-well, I am not sure about the naval department-and of the air department,

there have been heart-rending cases in Canada. There have been some very sad cases in this country.
I have in mind a case of a noble young man of my city, who was in the proper age category. When the time came, that young man enlisted immediately in the air force. He was sent to the manning pool at Toronto. He earned his commission, went overseas, and will never come back. But his father has been receiving calls for him to report, or else the mounted police will come and take him. That boy lies over yonder. That is the sort of thing which should never be allowed to happen. There are many men in that category.
Then, there are many more men in the category of those who have enlisted voluntarily, who have reported and gone into active service, but for whom calls are still coming. I know of the case of a young man, a>nd I shall be glad to give the minister his name privately; I do not wish to place it on the record. In this instance one could scarcely believe that what happened could be possible. This young man was called for service, and had enlisted weeks ago. He was actually working in the same building that housed the administrative offices of the department from which were being sent calls and threats addressed to him. One would scarcely believe that could be possible, but I know it is so.
Of course I believe that is an isolated case, and it might happen even in the best of regulated families. But I do suggest it is indicative at least of a failure of the recruiting authorities, in the early stages. Recruiting officers were out to get their men. When they got them, and had them sworn in, their duties were over, so far as they were concerned. Of course, that sort of thing should not happen.
I should like now to deal with a further part of this picture. That great total of 379,833 is not the whole story. The department got 608,642 replies from the 988,475 notices sent out. Then it proceeded to call the men for training. In the period covered by the minister's statement they called up 289,544. But 289,544 did not report for training.
They were medically' examined, too.

_ Those were men called up after the preliminary medical examination. Out of 289,544 there reported only 160,162, and there are unaccounted for in that category 128,882.- So

that you have that missing army, that potential army, according to the minister's own figures, of 379,833 plus 128,882, or a total of 508,715 missing men.
