propose to analyse. If last Wednesday the minister had given the authority of his position to those figures, there might be a different story. But I am reviewing what was supposed to be a complete statement of affairs made by the minister when he introduced these estimates. Since then there has been some tall thinking, because if you are to believe what the minister said last Wednesday, then the figures are nothing less than astonishing. They tell a story which is a disgrace to the Canadian people, and a disgrace to the government which is conducting the war effort. I leave that part of it with the minister, who may answer it if he will.
However, the fact remains that according to the minister's statement of last Wednesday there were 508,000 missing men. We got out of the total of 988,475 to whom notices were sent, how many? How many did the army actually get? The army actually got 126,963, who were accepted for training, or just over twelve per cent. What a situation that is!
And mind you, these men are not for active service overseas. They are for a perpetuation of two armies in this country, one at home, and an active army-a home army that ought never to have been, a home army, now that danger is receding, and has been receding month after month, and when danger of invasion is long past, a home army that will never see any fighting. And we are going to' keep those men in uniform, and in expensive military camps at a cost of hundreds of thousands of dollars every day to the taxpayers of Canada. What a farce is there, my countrymen! If the government had any realistic idea, of the situation, those men ought to be available for service where they can do: something-after we spend thousands of dollars upon them.
I should like to know how much it costs this country to enlist a man, call him up for active service, examine him physically, put him into the army, give him elementary training and secondary training, and send him off to some camp like that at Debert. In a year's time, how much has he cost Canada?
72537-260J
It would be interesting to have somebody give those figures. I suggest that it cost not less than $2,500 for every man.

Perhaps $3,500. That is a mere guess on my part because I do not know. In any event the amount is huge, and to what end have we made this expenditure? In the expectation of invasion? That is all poppycock. Everybody knows that. To the end that these men shall fight Canada's battle in the theatres of war where battles will rage? Not so long as hon. gentlemen opposite follow the policy that has characterized their actions for three and a half years. That is the situation to-day.
We would never have had this home army if the government had been a responsible government, if the government assuming to run the war and realizing that it was a global war had said, as they ought to have said, "The Canadian army is for service anywhere." No; the government did not say that, and the government have not said that yet. If the Canadian army is not called up to fight, and it will not be necessary, Canada will have played an inglorious part in this great struggle. That is not the future which I would have for the Canadian army. I would not want to see the Canadian army shed blood unnecessarily, as was done at Dieppe, but I want to see our army bear itself gallantly as representatives of Canadian patriotism in this great war, just as our friends from New Zealand, our friends from Australia, our friends from South Africa, our friends from the United Kingdom and our American cousins are doing.
We will analyse the statement which 'the minister has given to-night. In the meantime I have given figures which I have based upon the minister's previous statement. What becomes of the basis of the theory that this is the best system of national selective service that could possibly be devised? I say to the minister that the policy is an improvisation from day to day. It never has been a basically national policy. It is like Tqpsy; it grew up overnight. I can see that by the end of the war in the natural course of evolution we may have a full-fledged national selective service policy-three years too late. That is all I have to say.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, since this debate has been under way there has been general acknowledgment from all sides of the house that we were dealing with the most difficult problem that any democratic government at any time in the history of the world
War Appropriation-Labour

has had to deal with. On former occasions when this matter was being discussed hon. gentlemen pointed out to whatever minister was then in. charge of the problem of Canadian man-power in relation to war that the government had no man-power policy at all. Some hon,. gentlemen still .persist in that view. Almost without exception, every speaker on the opposite side has begun his remarks by congratulating the present minister. Without wanting to show needless discrimination, the most thorough critic of the government on the opposite side was the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker). When com gratulating the minister he prefaced his remarks-I think he was most fair in so. doing -by saying that the minister was dealing with the most difficult problem that any nation had to face at this time. It is in the light of this difficulty that the whole problem must be considered.
One could transpose the Hansard of this house into the congressional record of the United States, into the debates of the British House of Commons, into the debates of the Australian parliament, or into the debates of the South African parliament; one could read the debates of any of these parliaments, and one would almost think he was reading a discussion of the man-power policy of Canada. In considering this tremendously difficult problem we are dealing, not with milk bottles but with human beings who have family affiliations, who have financial interests, who have love of community, who have in their veins, as we all have, the persistent quality of love of freedom. That is why we realize that this problem is a tremendously difficult one. We find it difficult, and perhaps there may be, not justification but some extenuating circumstance in the fact that in those countries where the democratic process does not prevail, particularly Germany, where the individual is an ordinary commodity that can be shifted about and dealt with as though men and women were not human, they have had and have a manpower problem, although long before the war they were moving their men and women about in the fashion that total war envisaged. The fact is that in Germany to-day there is a bottleneck of man-power, even though they are able to call for assistance upon those countries which have been occupied by Hitler and his associates. If this is a problem in the totalitarian countries where there is as full a regimentation as possible, is it any wonder ' that we in this country should find it difficult? It is difficult, extremely difficult. The minister in his statement in chief indicated that

this was why he suggested to hon. members that they should offer criticisms of the present policy such as it is.
Constructive.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Someone suggests, constructive. I think on the whole that suggestions by hon. gentlemen opposite have been constructive, although they have consistently pursued the view that the government's manpower policy, which they now accept to be a fact, is nevertheless conceived on terms that suggest a day-to-day policy. If the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) had one theme running through his speech, it was that we had a day-to-day policy, a policy that was evolutionary; that we did not have a master scheme, that we simply day by day devised ways and means of dealing with the inevitable competition for men by the armed services, industry and agriculture. Of course it is a day-to-day policy. Of course it is evolutionary. Is there any hon. member who can think of a policy being otherwise conceived? Is there any country in the world, apart from the totalitarian powers, that has anything but a day-to-day policy? Can anyone envisage in a democratic! country the full utilization of manpower by the three branches .in terms of the ultimate sequence of the war? Of course not.
The hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) quoted Eric H. Biddle who, in the opinion of Mr. Ernest Bevin, has written some of the most serious studies of England's man-power policy. Let us see what Mr. Eric H. Biddle had to say only a short time ago about the character of Britain's man-power policy. I quote from a pamphlet entitled, "Man-power" a summary of the British experience, as follows:
A second type of assumption implicit in the British man-power programme was that the powers of compulsion should in practice be extended gradually, and should not be applied faster than an organization could be constructed to administer them efficiently. Thus the powers of compulsion have been used more to consolidate the positions won by persuasion than to initiate new methods for the assignment of skills. The government did not seek statutory powers to apply compulsion in civilian employment at the earliest stage. When it did seek these powers and got them, it proceeded to perfect its administrative organization, which was based to the greatest degree possible on voluntary cooperation and persuasion. And finally, it has applied its compulsory powers only to the extent necessary to channel the requisite skills to the place of greatest need. Only incidentally were these powers necessary to prevent the negligible minority from escaping their proper share of the national service obligation.
That was Britain's method; that is Britain's method. That is the day-to-day method, the

War Appropriation-Labour
evolutionary method, and that, as the hon. member for York-Sunbury has said, is exactly our method too. Yet Mr. Corson, whom the hon. member for Lake Centre will recall as perhaps the man in the United States who has the best knowledge of the man-power policy and the selective service system of the United States and Britain, has said that in terms of success Britain's policy of selective service Eomes first. In the same book, "Victory for Man-power", he says in speaking of bottlenecks and the muddles of the United States selective service system that both the United Kingdom and Canada serve generally as models for man-power mobilization in terms of war service. Therefore our policy, while not perfect, while day to day, is nevertheless not deserving of the carping criticism which sometimes one hears in this house and more particularly outside in these days.

Should to-night have relied on the minister's explanation of the figures previously given rather than allow to go out to the country the kind of limited understanding his speech will needlessly provoke.
The hon. member referred to the fact that we had a registration in 1940. He referred to the fact that there were imperfections in that registration. I believe there were im-fections which, if we had known of them then as we know of them now, would have been avoided, but hindsight is always better than foresight. The thing to remember is that since the national registration of 1940 there have been continuing subsequent registrations, and they deserve to be mentioned.
There have been special registrations of persons in insurable employment as of April, 1942; of unemployed males as of June, 1942; of women aged twenty to twenty-four as of September, 1942; employer's reports, January, 1943; registration of nurses, March, 1943; registration of men in designated age classes who had not received "order-medical examination", March, 1943; men employed in certain less essential industries and occupations, May, 1943. Third, there has been a continuing registration of the unemployed at local employment offices, September, 1942.
So that when one talks of the failure of the registration of 1940 as it is sometimes referred to, these other registrations should be borne in mind. While I have not and do not pretend to have the knowledge of this problem that the minister and his officials and many other hon. members have, because my contact with it has been of recent date, I want to say this, and perhaps I am sufficiently removed from the administration of the department to be able to say, that there is no group of civil servants in this country, first of all those located in Ottawa, who are devoting more of their time day and night in trying to perfect this system than the officials of the Department of Labour and of national selective service. The same thing applies to the outside personnel and the increased number of offices. The latter have been more than doubled and their staffs have been increased throughout the country. They have had imposed upon them a tremendous task, a task which they are gradually and more effectively falling into with greater efficiency and greater ease. As the minister said, and the hon. member for York-Sunbury concurred, these gentlemen would take second place to none in affirming that the men and women who serve in the selective service offices throughout the country are doing their utmost in this difficult problem to deal with the various orders and directives that come to them centrally from Ottawa.

I think the best way to analyse the difficulty of this problem is to examine the speech that has just been delivered. The hon. member for York-Sunbury was frank to say, and I admire his frankness, as he has said in practically every speech he has made in this house since the beginning of the war-I have analysed them all during the past two weeks- that his primary concern is to get men for the army. One can well understand that as being his concern. What he is concerned about is getting reinforcements. He is not so much concerned now with fitting round pegs into square holes. His primary interest in the problem of selective service and of man-power is to see that there is a constantly increasing flow of men into our armed services. With that I do not quarrel. But relate that to the general criticism that is levelled. We are told that we have three groups that are competing for men in this country-the armed services, industry and agriculture. You cannot have the sort of plan the hon. member for York-Sunbury was talking about if you think solely in terms of one of these competing groups.
The best way to illustrate that, I think, is to remind the committee of a speech made by the hon. member on April 20, 1942. His speech will be found at page 1752 of Hansard. The hon. gentleman had gone on in eloquent terms to urge the government to make sure, as we all want to do, that there would be an adequate flow of reinforcements, that Canada would be able to have in her armed forces a number of men commensurate with our strength, with our dignity, with our convictions. Pie urged us not to pursue in our attempt at patriotism a policy of expediency with individual cases. Then he cited a case, and here are the words:
Last week a woman, whose husband was ill, came to see me. She had a son eighteen years of age, who was the only support of her family, and he was being refused employment in New Brunswick under the provisions of the government's man-power policy.
I am not going to argue for one moment that that case was not deserving. I am not going to suggest that it did not merit the very attention which the hon. member for York-Sunbury wanted. But what I do wish to point out is this. Hon. gentlemen cannot urge in this house and in the country a man-power policy which will be rigid, which will be non-discriminatory, and at the same time rise in their places and make pleas for special cases.
Why not?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: I will tell the hon. member why not. I think it is perfectly obvious, but evidently I have not made myself clear, and I will do so for the hon. member, who usually does not require such elucidation.
I do not think the hon. gentleman has made himself clear.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Well,I am trying to explain it. I say that if you are to do what hon. gentlemen opposite want, and by compulsion take men and women and put them into places where it is thought they are best suited, you have not the right to say that there are instances where you should not pursue that policy. Either the policy is correct, or it is not. But the very incident quoted by the hon. member for York-Sunbury is a justification of our policy. We are not treating human beings as commodities; we are treating them as human beings. We recognize that that boy, the only support of his mother, had the right to special consideration. Under the kind of policy that Hitler has, under the kind of policy which some of the hon. gentlemen in this house advocate, you could not have that treatment. But this is why we have proceeded step by step, and also why we have not except in two instances applied the element of compulsion. We felt, and I support this view, that if we could get men to go into the armed services and into industry and into agriculture voluntarily, it is more effective to get them in that way than to put them in by compulsion. That is the reason why our policy is one of evolution; that is why it is a day-to-day policy meeting day-to-day needs; and if there is any hon. member who can suggest any other more effective method, I trust that in the course of this debate he will do so.
I suggest to the hon. gentleman that since the war broke out it' might have been a very good idea if they had had a plan, and that they have had no plan since the war broke out.
Order.
No policy and no plan.

That has been done by leadership.

That we do not have.

speechtext:
-Britain, a unitary state,, not having the same difficulties in transporting her -people, displays, as I am proud to rise in my place in this house and say, the shining example of an effective selective service system. She has had the advantage of a machinery which is over thirty years old. She has an unemployment insurance scheme which outdates ours by -many years. speechtext: But they have had an unemployment service office for ten years.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman says that we have. We had provincial offices. But the system was not integrated, and they were not part of a national scheme. That came
into being under the Unemployment Insurance Act. These extenuations may not be justification for the weaknesses of our policy, but they certainly are extenuations.
The hon. member for York-Sunbury made a plea for greater equality of sacrifice, saying that there are some parts of the country which are not giving as much as the others. I cannot quarrel with that. Not much is to be gained by saying where that persists. But can any hon. member here provide a yardstick by which- equality of sacrifice may be measured? Can anyone compare the heroism of the people of Stalingrad with ourselves at home? Can anyone compare the horrors through which the people of Poland have gone with any horrors of which we have personal experience? Can we compare ourselves with the people who were subjected to the blitz in Britain? Of course not. Equality of sacrifice is the thing that one should aim at, but merely to aim at it does not mean that equality can be realized. The fact is that the Canadian people in all walks of life, primarily those in our armed services, those who are serving in our war plants, the ordinary man and woman, the little man and woman in this country -and the rest of us, with all our weaknesses, with all our imperfections of governmental machinery, are nevertheless putting up an effort of which we shall in the terms of days to come have every reason to be proud rather than to be ashamed. It is in that spirit, I believe, that this whole policy should be looked at.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I simply say this. This policy is not perfect by any means. Some hon. gentlemen may say it should have come earlier, and perhaps many will find reason to agree with that. Some will say that there should be a greater amount of compulsion than has been exercised, and that, too, will be a fair issue. Remember, sir, it will only be an issue. Those who entertain the view that persuasion is better than compulsion may be perfectly honest in that view. That is the view which we are trying, and have been trying during these last years, to meet. Where compulsion has been found necessary it has been exercised. Faced with a coal emergency we have sought to exercise, with reason, prudence and understanding, because we are dealing with human beings, the phases of compulsion. With regard to certain non-essential occupations, without trying needlessly to disturb our people, at long last we have been obliged to disturb them and to ask them to leave their normal vocations, and, if they are within the military -ages, to go
War Appropriation-Labour

and serve in those places where they will more directly assist the government at this time of our peril.
That is the record. That is a policy in terms of estimates of man-power supply and requirements, a policy in terms of the allocation of supply, a policy in terms of control of employment, a policy in terms of improvement in efficiency of welfare and administration. The work that we have done, with respect, for instance, to the endeavour to bring recreation facilities to workers through cooperation with the provinces, our efforts with respect to day nurseries, particularly in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, trying thereby to introduce a greater and greater number of women into factory life-all that is part of a policy that is slowly perhaps but gradually making headway. And those hon. members who think we have not even now the sort of thing that was envisaged by a former director of national selective service, find it difficult, with the one sole possible exception of a suggested separate department, apart from full compulsion, to notice in the government's present man-power policy anything really distinguishable from that suggested by the former director of national selective service. I say that the problem has its difficulties. We are a democratic country, a people who are deep-rooted in the desire to be left alone. We do not like to be moved out of our jobs; we do not like to do things that disturb our family attachments or our community interests. But our people have done that very thing, and in its policy of bringing these things about, in the fashion it has, perhaps not always strong, perhaps not always as vigorous as some hon. gentlemen think it should be, nevertheless the government has pursued its course with vigour, with understanding and with results. I submit to you, sir, that nothing else counts.

In common with other hon. members I followed with great care and attention the address delivered by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Labour. As I listened to that speech I felt that the two problems that should be faced and that were referred to by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) were precisely the two problems which the hon. gentleman did not face in the argument he advanced. He said we could not expect to have equality of sacrifice. No one in this house can disagree with that statement. He spoke of the sufferings of the people of Stalingrad and of the sacrifices of those who to-day are serving in the various theatres of war. He said that their sacrifice and their heroism made impossible equality of sacrifice on the part of the people on the home front in Canada. With that fMr. Martin.]
statement no one can disagree. The argument advanced by the member for York-Sunbury was not based on the principle of equality of sacrifice; it was based on the question whether or not this government was assuring equality of opportunity for service by the people in every part of this dominion. The argument which he advanced was that since the National Resources Mobilization Act was brought into effect there never has been, and there is not now, equality of call in every province and in every part of the dominion. I shall deal with that not by figures of far-off months, but by reference to a table that was recently brought down in this house in the form of a return which shows the call-ups between October 31, 1942, and April 15, 1943, which conclusively establishes the fact, which neither the minister nor the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat has dared to try to answer, namely, that there is not now, nor has there been, equality of call in every military district in Canada, nor any reasonable approach to equality of call.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Take page 10.

I will take figures not in the reformed, revised, enlarged computation which it was found necessary to bring down to-night, because of the impossibility of any statistician arriving at any conclusion on the basis of the figures that were brought diown a week or so ago. The tables a week ago revealed a muddle. The tables brought down to-night reveal a muddle of the muddle and reveal no clarification whatsoever of the earlier ones. I will take the figures set out in a return brought down recently by the government. That will show exactly whether or not there has been equality of call.
The next point raised by the hon. member for York-Sunbury was that there was lack of enforcement of the law so far as the National Resources Mobilization Act was concerned. All of us admit that lack of enforcement of the law tends to disruption and confusion. I was surprised to find that that, too, was one of the things the parliamentary assistant did not answer. He dealt with many other matters, but the two subjects dealt with by the hon. member for York-Sunbury, namely, inequality of call in every province and in every part of Canada, and, second, inequality in enforcement, with the large numbers who are delinquent in consequence and amounting to hundreds of thousands, were not answered nor was there any attempt to answer them.
The other day, on June 23, the minister himself tried to answer the argument I had made on many occasions in this house, that

War Appropriation-Labour
there was inequality in the percentage of callups for men for military service in the different military districts. As reported at page 4030 of Hansard, he used these words:
The instructions to all mobilization divisions are to bring the men in the designated classes under the regulations as quickly as possible and to deal with them as rapidly as the machinery available permits. The districts vary in size. Some have greater difficulty in getting accommodation and staff. Therefore the speed of selection varies, but in the end the result sought for is obtained-that is, all men fit for service, in the designated class, who are not given postponement and have not volunteered for service in the armed forces are selected.
That statement is not in accordance with the known facts. The minister gave two reasons why there might be inequalities. The first reason was that the districts vary in size. What difference is there in the matter of callups on the basis of population because one district may be larger than another? That answer does not afford any defence for what is taking place. The second reason given was that some districts have greater difficulty in getting accommodation and staff. Well, Mr. Chairman, this same matter was dealt with by the Minister of National Defence at page 3059 of Hansard for May 26, when I drew to his attention the fact that there was inequality in call-ups, and that those districts in which the greatest number of volunteers were secured were the districts in which the largest percentage of men were being called up under the mobilization act. This is what the minister said:
Mr. Ralston: I do not requisition from particular districts. I ask for so many men to report at different depots. They can come from British Columbia, Halifax, anywhere at all; I do not designate the district from which they shall come.
Mr. Diefenbaker: Every one of the ministers says that some other minister is responsible.
Mr. Ralston: I do not think 1 am one who attempts to shelve responsibility.
Mr. Diefenbaker: No; the minister does not.
Mr. Ralston: I am asking if my hon. friend suggests that I dictate where the men shall come from?
Mr. Diefenbaker: I do not care who is dictating. I want an explanation from the responsible minister why this condition prevails.
Mr. Ralhton:	I am only saying my hon.
friend cannot get it from me.
Then a little later:
Mr. Ralston: What we do is to make a requisition or statement showing that we want so many men at such and such a depot.
And mark these words:
The men may come to these depots from any place in the dominion. National war services and more lately the Department of Labour, through its registrars and boards, decide what men shall be requisitioned.
The Minister of National Defence indicated that men are called from all over Canada; that regardless of the districts from which they are called they are concentrated in the various camps, without regard to the provinces from which they are called. We are in the position that no member of the government has answered the claim made by me on more than one occasion in this house, reiterated to-night by the hon. member for York-Sunbury, that there is not equality of call throughout Canada.
Let us take the facts revealed, not in the recently revised, enlarged or expurgated computations, -but those contained in a return brought down on June 17, 1943, in answer to a number of questions I had asked. I am going to place on record the information contained in this return, because it shows the facts as they are; it reveals the inequalities of the call-up and demonstrates that even yet there is no approach to equality of call in the various military districts of Canada. These were the questions:
1.	How many men, by military districts, w'ere requisitioned for by the Minister of National Defence for call-up under the National Resources Mobilization Act since October 31, 1942?
2.	How many notices were sent out pursuant to requisition?
3.	How many men, to whom notices were sent, reported?
4.	How many of those reporting received medical examination, and of these, how many passed?
5.	How many of the men to whom calls were sent were duly enrolled?
In the answer it is stated that the total requisitions, both new and supplementary, between October 31, 1942, and April 16, 1943, were 104,684. It sets out the numbers called in each military district, and then, in reply to paragraph 4, states that the following numbers were accepted:
"A" London	 2,419
"B" Toronto	 7,110
"C" Kingston	 1,072
"D" Port Arthur	 583
"E" Montreal	 6,413
"F" Quebec	 2,356
"G" Halifax	 2,995
"H" Saint John	 1,532
"I" Charlottetown	 419
"J" Winnipeg	 2,276
"K" Vancouver	 3,445
"M" Regina	 2,774
"N" Edmonton	 1,842
I have analysed these figures on the basis of the statements made in the February issue of Canada At War, page 22; I have arrived at the figure of the number of men available in each military district, after making allowance for the number of men who have enlisted, and I find that if there had been

War Appropriation-Labour

equality of call, in order to secure the men called up during this period, the rate of call from the available pool would have been 2-22 per cent. What I mean by that is this, that with all the available men remaining in the various military districts, after deducting from the pool as it existed at the time of registration, and as brought up to date by the subsequent registration, the numbers who are in the army whether voluntarily or under the mobilization act, the percentage of call would have been 2-22 per cent. What do we find? In district No. 1, London, the percentage of call was 2-41, or just a little over the average. In Toronto it was 2-78 per cent. In Montreal it was 1-8 per cent, or 34 per cent lower than the average call. In Quebec it was 1-16 per cent, or 91 per cent less than the call would be if it was equalized throughout Canada. In Halifax it was 4-2 per cent, or far above the average. In Saint John and Charlottetown combined rate was 3-8 per cent; in Winnipeg and Port Arthur combined, 4-16 per cent; in Vancouver, 2-87 per cent; in Regina, 2-2 per cent; in Edmonton, 2-13 per cent.
We find therefore that the same inequality in calls which was taking place prior to the month of October, 1942, is being continued in practice, and there is no defence by the government to the charge that there is no equality of call, excepting that the minister says there are two. very good reasons by way of defence. I have referred to those reasons, neither of which explains the situation as it is.
The other point dealt with by the hon. member for York-Sunbury was the question of the number who to-day are wandering in the byways of Canada, who have received a call, but who have not turned up. Mention was made by the parliamentary assistant to the question of national registration. He pointed out that there was national registration in 1940, and that there had been a number of registrations since that time.
Is there any member in the house who will say there has been any endeavour on the part of the government to enforce compliance with the national registration. I do not know how many prosecutions there have been. I speak for the province from which both the Chairman and I come when I say that the number of prosecutions in that province- and1 I speak subject to correction-does not exceed fifty. The only occasion when there is a prosecution for failure to register is when a man is brought up before the court on some charge or another, and it is found he has not a national registration card.
There has been no enforcement of the provisions of the national registration of 1940,
(Mr. Diefenbaker.]
and little or no enforcement since that time for non-compliance. There is only one way in which this question can be brought to a head, as I see it, and that is that once more there will have to be a national registration, and an enforcement to ensure strict compliance. I do not think it is possible to-day for the Minister of Labour or for any other minister of the government to know to what extent there has been an evasion of national registration.
I can give my hon. friend the figure immediately, if he would like to have it?
Yes, I would.
To date there have been 1,351 prosecutions, of which 1,326 have been won by the crown.
Is that in connection with national registration?
Yes, and 14,932 in the hands of the police at this time.

No, no; those figures do not answer me at all. Those are figures connected with prosecutions for failure to answer the call-up for military service. I am talking about prosecutions for failure to register under national registration.
Let me say this, too, that the figures the minister has placed before the committee show conclusively how indifferently evasion of the call-up is being enforced. I shall give figures in connection with the call-up, not from the revised list, but from the booklet "Canada at War", issued in February last by the wartime information board. The figures are to be found at pages 22, 23 and 24. They show the government admits that 135,890, of those called up, namely 1,028,753, never replied. They did not answer the call. And of the remainder, after deductions are made for those who received postponements, and for those proved medically unfit, there were 205,776 still unaccounted for. That makes a total of 341,000 men unaccounted for in December, 1942. Those are the studied figures sent out by the wartime information board. As a matter of fact, to-day the minister says there are only 13,000 or 14,000 delinquents in Canada.
I never said that. Fourteen thousand names have been handed to the police.

Thirteen hundred have
been already in court.

Fourteen thousand names have been handed to the police. Even in February, as shown at page 24 of this

War Appropriation-Labour
booklet, it was admitted that the total number of medical notices undelivered was 87,485; military training notices undelivered, 9,345, and cases pending, delinquents, or otherwise unaccounted for, 98,128. Those are the wartime information board's figures in February last, and they show the number admitted to be delinquents, out of approximately 1,000,000 calls, to have been 194,958 men.
If the government would admit that it is having difficulty; that it cannot enforce the law; that it has not the moral suasion; that it has not the necessary police force, and that it was endeavouring to enforce the law equally, then one would have more sympathy with the minister's department. But that is not the answer.
I wish now to refer to Mr. MacNamara's speech to the Academy of Political Science in New York, in which he gave various reasons why it is difficult to mobilize [DOT] man-power in Canada. In this speech, to which I referred the other day, he closes with these words:
We have felt our way slowly; are still feeling our way.
Well, Mr. Chairman, after four years of war are not the people of this country entitled to better than that? Can we not have a better answer than that with respect to inequality of call and inequality of opportunity of service for the people of this dominion? Can we not have a better answer than that we have felt our way slowly, and that we are still feeling our way?
When I read this speech I ask myself this question: What defence does the government offer to this speech wherein is set out the situation in Canada respecting man-power? What defence does it offer as to why there has not been the type of war effort Canada has a right to demand? On the first page he states that the situation in Canada is different from that in the United States. It states:
While time will not permit a detailed analysis of the differences and similarities between Canada and the United States, it seems advisable to mention some of the more significant items in any such comparison as a background against which you may consider Canada's manpower policy.
Like the United States, Canada is a federal union, but, because there are only nine provinces as against forty-eight states, the opinion of each province probably carries a greater weight in determining federal policy than does that of any single state.
That statement is a negation of the principles of the Canadian confederation, and a denial of the hopes of the fathers of confederation. That statement, translated into simple terms, means this, that in Canada any one province, be it Saskatchewan, or any

72537-26H
other province, may hold the government back, because of the greater influence possessed by one province in a confederation of nine, than one state in a confederation of forty-eight states.
Next follows something that is rather interesting, am admission of what we have contended on many occasions, that the government of this nation, in so far as the war is concerned, is a matter of government by order in council. This is what Mr. Mac-Namara said:
Most of Canada's war-time policies are expressed in orders in council comparable to your executive orders, passed by the cabinet under this authority and simply tabled in parliament.
It remained for the deputy minister to place before the people of the United States that which has been denied times without number in this house, that parliament has ceased to function in so far as the war-time policies of Canada are concerned, and that they owe their inception in orders in council. Then follows the strangest doctrine I have ever heard advanced by any Canadian. I know my hon. friends from Quebec are just as anxious as anyone else for equality of service.
Equality of privilege.

Equality of privilege and equality of opportunity for service. The deputy minister said:
Consequently all government policy has to run the gauntlet of democratic review, in that disapproval of any major policy would necessitate the resignation of the government and, unless the opposition could command a sure majority in the house, an appeal to the country in the form of a general election.
Although Canada like the United States is a land of many peoples, the fact that we spring chiefly from two main stocks. French and British, somewhat complicates, although it also enriches, our political and social life.
Certainly it enriches our political and social life. I continue:
Every government policy must be framed with due regard to their special rights-
That is true.
-and their convictions.
If that statement represents the viewpoint of the government, it denies the hope that this country will ever become united from the Atlantic to the Pacific, it denies an opportunity to the people of this nation to become Canadian, united, firm, strong and free under the British crown, united in their desire to dedicate themselves to common service and common sacrifice. I repudiate the doctrine enunciated in that speech. That will not make for true Canadianism. It is the type of doctrine
War Appropriation-Labour

that will tear this country asunder, will split our people apart, and will separate us, instead of bringing us together in the bonds of common sacrifice in war.
Is it not time that we gave to the people of all parts of Canada equal rights of service, so as thereby to enrich the Canadianism of which we are so proud? We should give an opportunity to every man and woman in every part of Canada to serve equally as nearly as possible. The people in the province of Quebec are perfectly willing to defend Canada. They accepted the National Resources Mobilization Act; they accepted the principle of service for the defence of Canada, but under the enforcement of the legislation to-day they are being denied the opportunity that the other eight provinces have, namely, the privilege and honour to march together regardless of racial origin in a union such as we have never known before.

The parliamentary
assistant to the minister tried to spread some sugar over the selective service policy when he termed it the master plan. The fact that the figures given on Wednesday have had to be revised this evening would seem to be a contradiction of what he was trying to say.
There was not a revision of figures.

We tried to base our argument on the figures that were given on Wednesday, and those that were given this evening make it rather difficult for us to estimate exactly what is going on. Why was not this explanation given on Wednesday?
In view of the confusion I thought I would give a simpler statement.

Apparently it was required, but it should have been given on Wednesday. I think it must be admitted that when the board in one province grants postponements to the extent of ninety-three per cent and the board in another province grants them only to the extent of sixty-one per cent, the average for the whole dominion being eighty per cent, there is something definitely wrong. I realize that there are difficulties in this selective service the same as there are in many of the things we are trying to do in this war, but there is something wrong when the board in one province shows a tendency not to grant postponements to this extent. The government should have rectified this. I cannot understand why this condition should have been allowed to exist for two or three years. It is unfortunate that Saskatchewan should

have been singled out in this way. I live in that province; I come in contact with the people, and I hear of cases such as that of the only son of a man practically blind1 who was taken off the farm, while two or three miles away two or three sons are allowed to remain. Such inequalities should not exist.
It seems to me the registration of 1940 was badly conducted. I do not know the minister's estimate of it, but I believe it was worth very little. The fact that selective service has operated under so many ministers in three years is proof of the situation we are getting into. The figures given this evening with regard to the number of call-ups and the number of cases in the hands of the police is evidence that the thing has been working poorly. Those who have not answered their call-ups have not been checked up soon enough. The difficulty with the board in Saskatchewan must have been owing to personnel. Who was the representative of the army sitting in with that board?
There is no representative of the army who is a member of the board, but the representative sitting in was Lieutenant-Colonel A. S. Redford.
Is he also officer commanding district depot No. 12?
I do not know.
I think we ought to have that information.
I shall be glad to get it for the hon. member. I let the army run their own show because I have a large enough undertaking myself.
It seems to me there is something wrong here, too.
He has never been in charge of district No. 12.
I asked whether he was an official of the district depot.
He has never been in charge. He is appointed by the military authorities to appear before the board in the interests of the defence department.
Was a similar representative of agriculture chosen to look after the interests of that industry? Could I have the name of that man?
Mr. Dawson.
Did he take the place of Mr. Milliken. who was appointed last January?

Yes.

War Appropriation-Labour

Mr. Milliken was an agricultural representative. He tried the job for two or three weeks and then gave up in desperation, because he had so many cases that he just could not handle them. I should like to know whether Mr. Milliken at the time of his resignation made any recommendations as to what should be done. His statement to the press was that it was such a terrific job he could not possibly handle it.
He was the legal representative of the pools out there? (
Yes.

He found that in view of his legal practice it was not possible for him to continue in view of representations that farmers would make through legal counsel. In place of Mr. Milliken we appointed Mr. Dawson who, I understand, is giving satisfactory service.

The point I wish to make is this. A good many people, as soon as they heard that Mr. Milliken had been appointed, wrote to him to ask for a postponement. They received no reply, because almost right away Mr. Milliken resigned, and their letters apparently were lost. A good many cases came to my attention which had received no consideration at all. The next thing the applicant knew he was called up. Who preceded Mr. Milliken?
I do not know. It was not under my jurisdiction then.

One of the most discouraging aspects of the whole situation was that the Prime Minister had made an announcement in March, 1942, to the effect that from then, on those engaged in agriculture would pretty well be kept in agriculture, and the onus of proof, according to that statement of the Prime Minister and according to the order in council rested with the board. It was the board that had to prove the men were not essential to agriculture, but the difficulty seems to be that they did not have to prove it to anyone. I ask the minister, to whom did the board have to prove that a man was not essential to agriculture?

As my hon. friend understands, the board is like a court, presided over by a judge of the supreme court. The board is the final authority under the regulations and it determines whether or not a man is essential to agriculture. The board takes no direction from the minister. It is a free agent in interpreting the law and regulations.

But according to the order in council the board had to .prove that the man was not essential to agriculture. Apparently it did not have to prove it to any one. There was no other court to which it had to prove it. It had to satisfy only itself.
The man had to prove to the board, which was headed) by a judge, that he was essential to agriculture.
That was prior to March, 1942.

That was always the
case prior to 1942.
No; a change was made in 1942, and the onus of proof placed on the board.
The man would state that he was essential to agriculture, and his statement would have to be accepted unless it could be proved otherwise.

If the minister will read the order in council and the statement of the Prime Minister, he will find that that is not correct. The onus of proof was on the board, and that is where the difficulty came in. There was no one to whom the board was responsible, and no appeal if anyone questioned its decision. The board was not responsible to anyone so far as I know. In fact, it is difficult even- to get the evidence that was placed before the board. About a year ago, on July 5, I put a question on the order paper asking for the evidence upon which the board had decided that a man was not essential to agriculture and was called up. That question was passed as an order for a return on July 13, 1942, and the order has not yet come down. Here is the master plan at work! I should like to know how many men have been called up from farms in Saskatchewan from March 23, 1942, up to, say a month ago.
I have not the figures in front of me but, if I can possibly get them, I shall be glad to do so.
I understand men are still being called up from farms in Saskatchewan.
If they are not essential to agriculture they are called up.
Medical notices are being sent out?	y

They get a medical examination, of course.
War Appropriation-Labour
Men. are still being called up.
Certainly.
How many in the past month?
I do not know. I will get the information for my hon. friend.
What is the basis for the board's figures as to how many notices of medical examination shall be sent out?

I thought I explained that'. The boards have been directed to move in on the designated age groups and call them up. We are approaching it in that way. There has not been any allotment. We are in a mopping-np process, calling up all men in the designated age classes. These men get their medical notices, but they can apply to a board for a postponement if they are essential to agriculture.

They can get a postponement if the board proves to its own satisfaction that they are essential to agriculture. In the spring of 1941 medical notices were sent out and a number of men took their medical examination. Then they were suddenly notified to return all their medical notices and to disregard that call altogether. They did so and thought there was no necessity then for making any application for postponement. Then here is the unfortunate thing that happened. The very same group on November 23 last received notices to report in Regina on November 25, with no opportunity at all to make application for postponement. I know of numerous cases of severe hardship as a result of that action.
I would say this, that the efficiency of the department will be judged by the equality with which they administer the regulations, and the record as far as Saskatchewan is concerned is one of which this department cannot be very proud. To call this a master plan is a piece of gross overexaggeration.

I endeavoured to
follow the minister's assistant this evening when he dwelt on persuasion rather than compulsion, but I was not able to follow him in view of what we have experienced in the last few years, because certainly we have had conscription for our home defence army-not persuasion at all. The Minister of National Defence and the Minister of National Defence for Air said that many of their best men had been young men- who had first received their call. Therefore I cannot see how there was any persuasion in these preliminaries; it was conscription for the army.

When we had the national registration in 1940 of men and women, certainly no plan was evolved for the use of our man-power and no estimate was made of the requirements of the armed forces or of industry or of agriculture. No plan was brought into being befitting Canada, not even as much as was done by our good neighbours to the south the moment war was declared. Those people certainly attempted to set up a plan, and they went a little further than we have gone yet in this fourth year of the wTar. One cannot help thinking that the Prime Minister and his ministers are still not assuming the responsibilities of their office with respect to the man-power problem to-day. There are, I believe, some 70,000 recruits in this country to-day who have been drafted. There is a difference of opinion as to what should be done with them, whether they should be in other and more useful employment or whether they should be available for any theatre of war. I know that in this regard, on another item, the hon. member for Brantford City (Mr. Macdonald) recently suggested that they should be sent to Alaska in order that United States troops could be relieved to do the fighting of the united nations in active theatres of war. I am sure that no red-blooded Canadian would feel proud of that suggestion, and we should not countenance it.
As to the matter of conscientious objectors, the statement has been made that in a very recent period 500 have been sent into Manitoba. I believe it was represented to the minister and to the government that this approximate number were required for beet production alone in that province. I know also that officers of the minister's department are in a quandary as to which is the most essential place for these men, whether it would be in this beet industry, or in the production of cereals, dairy products and bacon on the other farms of that province. In checking the minister's statement, I notice that he says, as reported in Hansard, at page 3937, that the mobilization boards no longer direct the placement of these men; they simply grant postponements. What cooperation is there between these boards and the minister's selective officers? It seems to me that up to date there is a distinct overlapping there. The mobilization board, when a man is called, hears the man's request for postponement. I assume it takes notes and keeps a record of all that evidence. I should like to know whether that is turned over to the selective officer, or what becomes of it, and if it would not be more beneficial that these selective boards should direct where that man should go at that particular time.

War Appropriation-Labour
The minister has said that young men are called if they are not essential to agriculture. My understanding is that every young man, when he comes of age under the call, whether he is a farmer or not, does receive his call.

He receives medical
examination.
XIr. ROSS (Souris): And does he not have to report to the board, if he is fit?
He has to apply for postponement, of course.
And if he does not ask for postponement he goes to the armed forces whether he is essential in agriculture or not?
I do not know.

Well, I think the minister should know, and I think he does know.
XIr. MITCHELL: Well, now, I do not know. Let us be perfectly honest. I am not going to mislead my hon. friend. Here are the three steps. The man gets his notice; he receives his medical examination; and if he applies, he obtains a postponement. He has to ask for it, and it is the natural thing to do if the man has a tongue in his head. If I did not want to go in the army, I suppose it is the course I would take, though I may say that if I were ten years younger I would not be standing here. But if the fellow did not want to go in the army, surely, when he went before that board he would ask for postponement. I mean, that is no secret in this country.
XIr. ROSS (Souris): The minister's statement is still very confusing. He has sitting before him his deputy minister and other assistants who, I am fairly sure, can answer this more definitely than the minister has attempted to do. This statement is rather misleading to the people of this country, because I know young men on the farms who are required on the farms but who are receiving their call and reporting to the board.
I just said that.

I understood the minister to say, if they were essential to agriculture, they do not do so. But this is the system which the government are working in order to get volunteers for the army. Certainly many young men who to-day are essential on the farms are not going to ask for postponement. As the minister has just hinted, he would not do it; neither would I do it if I received a call; in fact, I do not think either one of us would wait until we received a call. But if we did, certainly, with our pals over there we would not want to ask for postponement. And many of these young men to-day are not asking for
postponement, despite the fact that they are urgently needed on the farm. I say that the government is not fulfilling its responsibility in that I know of young men who have been operating their own farms, and who are of that call age, who this spring did not operate their farms though they would have done so had they some definite assurance that they could carry on for a year. Under the present system all they can receive is a postponement for six months. That is a most indefinite arrangement for any man who has to plan to-day for the production of foodstuffs to operate on. If the Minister of Labour will not agree with me, certainly the Minister of Agriculture will.
I will not agree that they get six months' postponement.
What do they get?
They get a postponement until further call if they are essential to agriculture.
But they are not assured of anything over six months, are they?
Oh, yes, they are assured until further call, which may take them to the end of the war.
They do not know when the next call will be.

Well, they do not get
another call unless there is new information.
That is a new arrangement, is it not?

If I may put it in a
sentence to my hon. friend, in agriculture they get indefinite postponement; in industry, the maximum is twelve months and the minimum six months. That is the whole thing, simply stated.

I shall not go into the
question of policy. Most of the complaints received from my province arise, I believe, on account of lack of experience of men in the selective service branch. Perhaps that is inevitable by reason of the number who have been engaged and the kind of work they have to do. I think it was the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) who asked the minister early in the evening if he had practical men to review or pass on the ability of the men to do certain work. I believe that is a very proper thing to do. I do not think a doctor can judge, absolutely at least, whether a man can work in a logging camp or in a mine or at any other employment where hard physical labour is required. I have before me
War Appropriation-Labour

in concrete form cases which a certain firm employing help in Vancouver took up with the national selective service after the second compulsory transfer order. I have the names, the numbers, and all other particulars, but I will not give the names. In case A, as I will eall it, the party has 'been known to the writer of the letter and to his company for quite a few years. He has suffered from extreme eye trouble since his early childhood. He has been under treatment for a considerable time and is still under treatment from Doctor Graham Elliott of that city, who has started him on a series of artificial fever treatments through another medical practitioner, which treatments cost $36 and necessitates his going into hospital. The writer goes on to state:
At the present time this man is practically blind in one eye and has very limited vision in the other. He has done no reading for over six months and does no writing. Until March last year he had been unable to take employment. At that time, when he had sufficient vision to get around, we found a job for him in eur hardware storeroom where he has served a useful purpose ever since. We of course allow him time off for his treatments, when his doctor recommends them.
Here is the disposition the selective service made. The officials of the selective service board slated him for a lumber or mining camp. The man explained his regrettable inability to consider either. The officials then wanted him to go to the shipyards where they would find him a nice easy job in the shade counting rivets. The man explained about his eyes and the fact that he was still taking treatment.
Then we come to another case, that of a furniture salesman, who had his rejection slip dated October 15, 1942, category E, permanently unfit. He has never done any labouring in his life. He has never been in the woods or in a lumber camp. The official is sending him to a lumber camp and has told him cheerfully that if he does not sign to go voluntarily they will drag him.
Anyone who knows anything about lumbering in British Columbia knows it is work for young able-bodied men. Before the war, only young -men were accepted there. It is an extremely hazardous occupation, much more so than lumbering in eastern Canada, and to suggest that a man should go to the lumber camps in British Columbia without having had any lumbering experience, and being too old and in poor physical condition, is simply to make him a menace both to himself and to those who would be working with him.
The next case-the name and number are given in each case-is that of a man who applied to -the air force and the navy prior to getting his army refusal. He was refused 
entrance into the armed forces on account of a heart condition. He visited the selective service board a second time and was told by the official who interviewed him that the medical board had decided that he should accept work in a logging camp. The man refused to accept -the ruling, and he was told again that he either had to accept it or they would compel him to do so.
I suggest that in such cases there should be a committee of loggers. They may not be qualified from the medical point of view, but I am sure they would know whether a man was able to work in a logging camp or not, because they would have to work with him. In cases of this kind, where a man is slated for some industry, such as logging, or any other activity of that kind, a practical committee of people who know what the industry is like should be asked to say what they think of the possibilities of the man being fit for that kind of work.

Those two gentlemen had the right to appeal to the court of referees against the decision of -the selective service officer. I know the gentlemen comprising labour representatives on the -board in Vancouver:	G. Price, Canadian Congress of
Labour; E. Morton, Canadian Congress of Labour; B. Showier, Trades and Labour Congress; R. H. Neelands, Trades and Labour Congress; R. Gervin, Trades and Labour Congress, and E. Smith, Trades and Labour Congress. The men to whom the hon. member has referred could have appealed to them.

The minister did not answer the question in regard to the liaison between the mobilization board and the selective service office. I said there was duplication there, and I should like to know how the two offices operate.
Representatives of the selective service attend the meetings of the mobilization -board1.
They sit in on every meeting?

Yes. We felt that the selective service covered all the ramifications of industry and agriculture, and we thought that if we took that from the mobilization board it would be better. All they do is to adjudicate the man as a conscientious objector and he is turned over to the selective service, who direct him.

The selective service officer has all the evidence of that kind.

On page 3954, of
Hansard, giving the tables which the minister submitted, there appears to me to be a point that is not answered. The number of men called is given as 988,475. They were called for medical examination. Some did not turn up, but the number examined was 608,642. Then we find that 233,224 requested postponements; 190,550 postponed and the number in effect, 100,973. That means that the number granted and the number in effect total 291,523. Are all these postponements?
Mr. MITCHELL; Yes.
Mr. ROSS (St. Paul's); So that out of the 608,642 examined we have 289,544 called for military service, and out of that number only 160,662 turned up. That leaves about 129,000 to be accounted for. In the statement the minister says:
Voluntary enlistments, as well as postponements, account for most of the difference of 129.000 between the numbers called for military training and those reporting.
I do not know where postponements enter into this. What happened to the 129,000? That is what I should like to know.

They are in the army
or in the navy or air force.
Are there 129,000 who enlisted voluntarily?
Five hundred and fifty thousand.
That is a most extraordinary thing.
It may be extraordinary, but they are in the army.

The number called was 988,000 odd, and the number examined
608.000,	and out of the 608,000 that turned up you have 129,000 that you cannot account for. We do not know where they are.
They did not have to turn up if they went into the army.
I should like to ask the Minister of Agriculture how he knows they went into the army, and if he can tell me just why they went into the army.

Because I was the minister in charge of the registration the hon. gentleman is talking about, at the time it was made. There were 54,000 men who were enlisted at that time, which number added to the
988.000,	makes the total registered who were of military age. Since that time men have been called, and they have enlisted in the army and did not have to report to this board.
But they did report to be examined.

Not the number over the
608,000.

They are part of the 608,000 who did report to be examined; and out of the 608.000 we have only accounted for the number I mentioned. I think that this is a farce of a statement, which does not give us anything at all. It is just a lot of figures that no one knows anything about, not even the government. They are trying to make excuses for the whole thing, but here you have
988.000	who were called, and you have 608,000 who responded, which leaves 380,000 about whom we know nothing. We know that some of those are in the army, that no doubt some of them have died and so on, but there were
608.000	examined during that time. What has happened to them? Then we have these
289.000	who were called, who had notices sent out to them. Nothing has been said during the debate, so far as I know, about any of the notices going astray in regard to these
289.000	men. They were examined and they were called; notices went out to them, but we never heard from 129,000 of them, and we do not know anything about them. No one knows anything about them, not even the government. The minister tries to make excuses for this state of affairs and goes away back to 1940, when he was in charge of the registration. I think he did a pretty good job at that time; I know I helped him all I could, as we all did. Perhaps I was one of the first members of this house to call for a national registration; that was away back in 1940. Do hon. members remember the registration cards we had to fill out, with all the questions on it; asking city people if they could milk cows, and all that sort of thing? By the way, I should like to ask the minister if he was responsible for drawing up that card and asking all those questions to find out if people in the cities could milk cows, and so on.
Order.

Did someone speak? The whole thing is just like that; some ghost here behind me said something; I do not know what it was, and that is the whole situation as far as I can see it. The point is that the government never wanted to get down to compulsory national selective service anyway. They made up their minds they were going to do this whole thing by evolution; they were going to go away back to the old monkeys and see if they could not get some of the monkeys to become men. Thank heaven we had a tremendous number of men who wanted to

volunteer and who did so. The answer to the whole question is that the government are not interested in where these 128,000 men may be; they are missing, but no matter. You can take this whole table and it is not worth the powder to blow it up; it is the same, as a matter of fact, as the government's national selective policy.
As I was listening to the hon. member for Essex East, who is the parliamentary assistant to the minister, I thought of the words I used on Friday night in describing the policy of the government. First, I said it was vaporous. Well, it was vaporous when the hon. member spoke to-night; there is no question about that. The next word I used-perhaps I did not go far enough-was that it was vacuous. Well, you know the dictionary meaning of "vacuous"; I believe it means empty, without anything in it, and that was what I thought of as I listened to the minister's parliamentary assistant. I do not think he is quite that bad, but there you are. It will be remembered that the hon. member for Vancouver Centre criticized me the other night for not saying enough, but the third word 1 used in describing the policy of the government was that it was vacillating. Well, did he vacillate to-night. That is exactly what he did; and then when he got through with his speech he said, "We won't use compulsion. We never have, and we do not want to have compulsion in this thing at all. We are going to continue on a voluntary basis." Then, when I asked him a question, as to whether they did not have compulsion, he replied, "yes, but only in two cases." Well, those two cases are for home defence, and for everyone between the ages of sixteen and sixty-five. There you are; that is the whole thing. Here is your list, and it is not worth anything; the figures on it do not mean a thing.
You are making quite a speech on it.

I cannot hear the hon. gentleman. I rather like him; he is a pretty good minister of agriculture, but he is a better politician. He has the province of Saskatchewan right in the palm of his hand, or he thinks he has. Wait until the next election comes along; perhaps he will find that it is not in the palm of his hand as he thought. He is clever, however, and I like to hear him speak in this house. I believe he is a smarter man than we give him credit for being, and I am sure he will say these things are as I have described them, that these figures in this table are worthless and do not mean a thing.
I will ask him the question: does he not admit that?
